What The Building An Affordable California Act Means, Practically
What the Building an Affordable California Act Means, Practically
An update and analysis of the most significant CEQA reform in 50+ years.
January 22, 2026
On December 26, 2005, the California Chamber of Commerce received an official Title & Summary (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/Title%20and%20Summary%20%2825-0023A1%29.pdf) from the Attorney General’s office for the Building an Affordable California Act (https://buildaffordableca.com/) (referred to here as the “Affordable CA”), and began signature gathering the first week of January. Early response has been strong—California voters are eager to sign a petition that cuts delays and lowers the cost of housing, electricity, and other everyday necessities. The Chamber is well on its way to qualifying Affordable CA for the November 2026 ballot, with signature collection on track to conclude by mid-April.
Based on our combined decades of experience advising, entitling, litigating, and defending projects subject to the California Environmental Quality Act (“CEQA”) throughout California, we have reviewed Affordable CA from a legal, procedural, and implementation perspective. Our analysis reflects extensive, first-hand experience with CEQA compliance, agency review, administrative records, and judicial review at every stage of project development.
Affordable CA represents the most comprehensive and consequential CEQA reform in more than 50 years. It eliminates open-ended delays by imposing enforceable timelines on all reviewing agencies, creates predictability in permitting processes through reliance on objective standards and vested rights, and curbs abusive litigation practices that delay projects without environmental benefit. Unlike prior CEQA reforms, which relied on narrow exemptions or project-specific streamlining, Affordable CA delivers systemwide, enforceable process reforms across eight essential project categories.
Based on our analysis, we conclude that the Building an Affordable California Act is legally sound, carefully calibrated, and extraordinarily effective. If enacted, it would materially reduce approval timelines and litigation risk for essential projects — often by multiple years — while preserving meaningful environmental review, public participation, and strong worker and tribal protections.
Core Reforms & Essential Projects
Affordable CA applies its reforms to a defined set of essential projects central to California’s affordability, climate, and public safety goals, including:
Housing : New single-family homes, apartments, senior and student housing, supportive and farmworker housing, and conversion of commercial buildings for residential use.
Public Health : Hospitals, community clinics, and medical office facilities that expand access to care.
Clean Energy : Solar, wind, geothermal, clean hydrogen, battery storage, fuel cells, clean carbon capture, upgrades to the electric grid, transmission lines, and EV charging networks.
Water Infrastructure : Water-quality treatment, groundwater recharge, water recycling and desalination plants, dams, stormwater capture, and other projects that deliver safe drinking water and strengthen California’s drought resilience.
Education Facilities : K–12 schools, community colleges, public and private nonprofit colleges and universities, including CSU/UC campuses, labs, and student support facilities.
Public Safety & Wildfire Resilience : Fire and police stations, vegetation management, undergrounding utilities, home hardening, and fuel break maintenance.
Transportation : Road repairs, bridges, public transit expansions, bike and pedestrian safety projects, and electric vehicle infrastructure.
Broadband & Digital Access : Fiber-optic and wireless broadband projects connecting underserved and rural communities.
Importantly, Affordable CA applies not only to the primary project, but also to the ancillary infrastructure required to place the project into service, including access roads, interconnections, sewage systems, pipelines, substations, etc. This ensures streamlining applies to the entire project delivery pathway, rather than allowing projects to be stalled through separate, sequential approvals.
Streamlined Approvals
1. Enforceable Timelines Across the Entire Approval Process
For the first time, CEQA timelines are mandatory and enforceable from application submittal through final approval for all types of CEQA documents.
Application Completeness . Agencies have 30 days to determine completeness or the application is deemed complete by operation of law. Any incompleteness notice must include a single , exhaustive list of missing items. Applicants have 90 days to cure identified deficiencies, then agencies receive an additional 30-day review period for any resubmittals. Any incompleteness finding may be appealed and must be resolved within 60 days . These requirements eliminate serial information requests and prolonged front-end delays.
CEQA Review Timelines . Once an application is complete, agencies must select the appropriate CEQA pathway within 30 days and complete environmental review within fixed deadlines:
90 days for exemptions and addenda
180 days for NDs/MNDs
365 days for EIRs
If an agency misses a deadline, the applicant may force a public hearing requiring final action within 60 days.
Concurrent and Coordinated Permitting. Once CEQA review is complete, all other permits, authorizations and approvals required for the same project by other agencies must be issued within 90 days of application completeness or, for exempt projects, within 90 days of the exemption determination . This prevents sequential permitting delays after CEQA compliance has been achieved.
Phased Approvals. Components of a qualifying larger project may proceed independently under Affordable CA timelines, allowing essential projects to advance in phases even if individual phases would not qualify on their own.
Preserves Lead Agency Decision Authority . Importantly, while Affordable CA enforces strict timelines it does not force project approvals. State and local agencies retain full authority to approve, reject and condition projects.
2. Vested Rights
Affordable CA restores predictability by requiring agencies to evaluate projects based solely on the laws, regulations and written standards in effect at the time of application submittal, including statutes, regulations, ordinances, and routinely applied thresholds of significance. This prevents midstream policy shifts or unwritten expectations from derailing pending projects. Applicants may voluntarily waive vested rights if they elect to proceed under newer standards.
3. Streamlined Alternatives Analysis
Affordable CA narrows the required alternatives analysis under CEQA to:
One applicant-proposed feasible alternative
The required “no project” alternative
The measure establishes a presumption that the applicant-proposed alternative satisfies CEQA’s feasibility requirement. This reform addresses one of the most common sources of delay, expanded administrative records, and litigation risk, often driven by demands to evaluate speculative alternatives that are not economically, technically, or legally feasible.
4. Firm Public Comment Periods
Affordable CA provides clear, enforceable public comment timelines:
20-day public comment period for NDs and MNDs
45-day public comment period for EIRs
Late comments are excluded except in limited circumstances involving information that could not reasonably have been raised earlier. Rights to comment at public hearings, even those after the comment period, are preserved. Continued hearings must be set to a date certain and do not reopen comment periods, preserving meaningful public participation while preventing procedural gamesmanship.
Faster, Fairer and More Predictable Judicial Review
1. Judicial Review Shot Clock
CEQA challenges must be filed within 30 days of the notice of determination or exemption . Courts must resolve CEQA challenges, including appeals, within 270 days , subject to a 90-day extension.
2. Severance – Only Fix What’s Broken
Affordable CA replaces CEQA’s all-or-nothing remedy structure. If a court identifies a flaw in one portion of a CEQA document, it may require correction of only that issue while allowing legally compliant portions of the project to proceed on schedule.
3. Objective Standards for Judicial Review
Courts may only overturn a project approval if the lead agency failed to comply with objective, written standards in effect at the time of application submittal. Subjective criteria or unpublished standards may not be used to invalidate approvals.
4. Substantial Evidence Standard
All CEQA documents must be upheld where supported by substantial evidence in the record.
Maintains California’s Strong Environmental, Tribal & Labor Protections
Affordable CA does not exempt projects from CEQA or from compliance with any other state or federal environmental law, and all substantive environmental protections remain fully intact, including the Clean Water Act, Clean Air Act, Endangered Species Act, and California Coastal Act. The measure preserves and strengthens tribal consultation under Assembly Bill 52 by requiring earlier engagement and incorporating Tribal Traditional Knowledge into the consultation process. Affordable CA also maintains California’s strongest labor standards, including AB 130 requirements for essential housing projects and Environmental Leadership Development Project-level labor standards for all other essential projects.
Bottom Line
Affordable CA fundamentally changes the risk profile of building in California by imposing enforceable timelines, objective review standards, and predictable judicial remedies. Based on our experience, we believe Affordable CA will cut years — not months — from project timelines, reduce carrying costs and enable California to deliver housing, infrastructure and essential services at scale without sacrificing environmental integrity or worker protections .
The Building an Affordable California Act represents a once-in-a-generation opportunity to realign CEQA with its intended purpose. We believe the measure is legally sound, carefully drafted, and urgently needed, and we encourage serious engagement with this effort, including consideration of support for its placement and passage on the November 2026 ballot.
[This is a summary for general information and discussion only. It is not a full analysis of the matters presented and should not be relied upon as legal advice. Readers should consult a lawyer regarding the applicability of Affordable CA to a specific project.]

Summary of California Chamber of Commerce Initiative
to Amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA)
Overview
The California Chamber of Commerce is propounding a statewide ballot initiative that
significantly rolls back environmental protections guaranteed by the California Environmental
Quality Act (CEQA). Officially titled “Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects,” the
Initiative weakens environmental review requirements for a broad range of projects, including
major infrastructure developments, to the benefit of developers. It also limits the ability of
communities to advocate for necessary public health protections, exposes public agencies to
increased liability risks, and strips courts of the power to issue a meaningful remedy when
CEQA is violated.
“Essential” Projects Covered by the Initiative
The Initiative applies to eight categories of projects, each labeled “essential”: housing, energy
infrastructure, water infrastructure, public health, public safety, transportation, educational
facilities, and broadband internet.
Each category encompasses a broad range of project types. Some of the most consequential
include:
• Major transportation infrastructure projects, including highways, bridges, interchanges,
tunnels, and ferry terminals;
• Major energy projects, including municipal solid waste conversion projects, landfill gas
facilities, dairy biogas projects, and electrical transmission systems and infrastructure;
• Major water infrastructure projects, including dams, reservoirs, canals, desalination
plants, and other water system components;
• Residential and specified mixed-use projects located anywhere in the state, including
large-scale developments in fire-prone sprawl areas; and
• Wildfire risk reduction projects, including vegetation management and fuel reduction
(potentially including forest clear-cutting).
The Initiative also covers all ancillary infrastructure components included in the qualifying
project’s application as part of the “whole of the project.” These ancillary components could
include, for example, wastewater treatment centers (ancillary to geothermal sites and water
systems) or major gas pipelines (ancillary to landfill gas energy projects).
The Initiative does not apply to new oil or natural gas production facilities, the Delta
Conveyance Project, nuclear facilities, high-speed rail systems, or jails and other detention
facilities.
2
Initiative’s New Rules for “Essential” Projects
1. Eliminates Longstanding Principle Favoring Environmental Protection
The Initiative states that its language should be interpreted and implemented to “afford the fullest
possible weight to the interest of, and the approval and realization of, essential projects.” This
reverses CEQA’s bedrock principle that the law must be interpreted to afford the fullest possible
protection of the environment.
2. Makes Procedural Changes
The Initiative provides new procedural requirements that restrict environmental review,
including but not limited to the following:
• It tightly limits the duration of public comment periods for most environmental
documents and provides that these comment periods can be extended only by court order
(an exception to this limitation exists where the lead agency is also the project applicant).
As a result, comment deadlines will become unreasonable for many projects. The new
rules specify:
o A maximum of 20 days for comments on negative declarations and mitigated
negative declarations (rather than a minimum of 20 days, or 30 days if state
agency review is required, as current law provides).
o A maximum of 45 days for comments on environmental impact reports (EIRs)
(rather than a minimum of 30 days, or 45 days if state agency review is required,
as current law provides).
Note: Comment periods are the principal opportunity for regulatory agencies and the
public to request information about a proposed project and to suggest mitigation
measures. Commenting agencies include “trustee agencies,” which must comment on a
proposed project’s effect on wildlife and other resources, and “responsible agencies,”
which have permit authority over projects. The new maximum time periods will reduce
the public’s and agencies’ ability to provide informed feedback and seek vital
information.
• It greatly expands the number and types of development projects subject to the strict
requirement that agencies determine the completeness of development applications
within 30 days. If a determination is not granted within that period, the application is
automatically deemed complete, limiting information that agencies can require of the
applicant in the future.
• It requires responsible agencies to act on project applications within 90 days of a
complete application, or within 1 day after the lead agency approves the project,
whichever date is later. This could make it more difficult for responsible agencies to
ensure that environmental documents prepared by lead agencies are sufficient for their
purposes, which could delay the issuance of necessary environmental permits.
3
• It eliminates the requirement for consultation with California Native American tribes that
are not federally recognized.
• It allows qualifying projects that are currently in the approval pipeline to take advantage
of the new relaxed rules. Applications can be withdrawn and resubmitted. Relatedly, it
provides that all projects deemed complete prior to the Initiative’s effective date shall
remain complete, even if the applicant has significantly altered the project since
submitting its application.
3. Allows Developers to Sue Public Agencies Under CEQA
The Initiative would create a new right of action for applicants to sue public agencies that deny
their projects. This represents a major change in the law that could significantly increase
litigation under CEQA, cost public agencies more in attorney fees, and pressure them to issue
project approvals even when the project might harm local communities and the environment.
Except for specified housing projects, CEQA does not currently allow applicants to sue over
project denials.
4. Weakens Standards for Environmental Review
Background: Under current law, CEQA requires that lead agencies determine whether a
proposed project’s environmental impacts are “significant.” If the lead agency concludes the
project will cause a significant impact, CEQA mandates that it adopt mitigation measures to
reduce that impact to a level of insignificance. Notably, CEQA requires agencies to use
“thresholds of significance” that are based on up-to-date scientific information and designed to
uncover the actual harm that a proposed project will cause.
What does the Initiative do?
The Initiative requires that the lead agency determine a proposed project’s significant impacts
based solely on compliance with “existing laws.”
• “Existing laws” mean formally adopted legal requirements in statutes, regulations, rules,
standards, or ordinances that were in effect when the application was submitted. The
Initiative does not require that these laws/standards be designed to disclose significant
harm to the environment.
• The Initiative creates narrow exceptions, allowing an agency to base its significance

Summary of California Chamber of Commerce Initiative
to Amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA)
Overview
The California Chamber of Commerce is propounding a statewide ballot initiative that
significantly rolls back environmental protections guaranteed by the California Environmental
Quality Act (CEQA). Officially titled “Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects,” the

major infrastructure developments, to the benefit of developers. It also limits the ability of
communities to advocate for necessary public health protections, exposes public agencies to
increased liability risks, and strips courts of the power to issue a meaningful remedy when
CEQA is violated.

The Initiative applies to eight categories of projects, each labeled “essential”: housing, energy
infrastructure, water infrastructure, public health, public safety, transportation, educational
facilities, and broadband internet.
Each category encompasses a broad range of project types. Some of the most consequential
include:
• Major transportation infrastructure projects, including highways, bridges, interchanges,
tunnels, and ferry terminals;
• Major energy projects, including municipal solid waste conversion projects, landfill gas
facilities, dairy biogas projects, and electrical transmission systems and infrastructure;
• Major water infrastructure projects, including dams, reservoirs, canals, desalination
plants, and other water system components;
• Residential and specified mixed-use projects located anywhere in the state, including
large-scale developments in fire-prone sprawl areas; and
• Wildfire risk reduction projects, including vegetation management and fuel reduction
(potentially including forest clear-cutting).
The Initiative also covers all ancillary infrastructure components included in the qualifying
project’s application as part of the “whole of the project.” These ancillary components could
include, for example, wastewater treatment centers (ancillary to geothermal sites and water
systems) or major gas pipelines (ancillary to landfill gas energy projects).
The Initiative does not apply to new oil or natural gas production facilities, the Delta
Conveyance Project, nuclear facilities, high-speed rail systems, or jails and other detention
facilities.

CEQA Reform Qualifies for the Ballot: What to Know About the Building an Affordable California Act
July 15, 2026 - E-Alerts (https://www.rutan.com/category/e-alerts/)

On June 25, 2026, the Building an Affordable California Act (“BACA”), a statewide measure sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce, officially qualified for the November 2026 General Election ballot. The initiative will appear on California ballots this November as Prop 45. If passed by voters, BACA would reform the California Environmental Quality Act (“CEQA”) to create a broad category of “essential projects” that are entitled to a narrower environmental review process, the option to engage in a streamlined project alternatives analysis and more limited judicial review in the event of a project challenge. Early polling shows BACA garnering significant support among California voters, with 73 percent of likely voters indicating their support for the measure in a recently released poll.
BACA Streamlines Environmental Review for Essential Projects
BACA applies only to developments that qualify as “essential projects.” Specifically included are “essential housing projects,” which the law defines as housing projects including residential units only, residential mixed-use projects, commercial-to-residential conversions, subdivisions consisting of residential units or unimproved residential lots, and a number of specific housing categories including transitional housing, student housing, and senior housing. Other types of essential projects include qualifying water, clean energy, public health, public safety, broadband Internet access, education facility, and transportation projects. Essential projects utilizing BACA’s CEQA review provisions, except for housing projects under 85 feet above grade, must pay prevailing wages to all construction workers.
BACA would modify certain procedures and time limits for environmental review of essential projects. First, agencies will have 30 days to determine whether an essential project application is complete. If the agency fails to meet the completeness deadline, then the essential project application will automatically be deemed complete.
Once an agency has determined whether the project will require an Environmental Impact Report (“EIR”), Mitigated Negative Declaration (“MND”) or negative declaration, or than an exemption applies, the measure imposes various deadlines for the agency to make a final determination, which run from the date the application is deemed complete: 365 business days to certify an EIR, 180 business days to adopt a negative declaration, and 90 business days to make a final exemption determination. If the agency fails to meet these deadlines in making a final determination, the applicant has the option of requesting a meeting or hearing, which the agency would be required to hold within 60 days and either approve or deny the project at the meeting, and thereafter maintains an express right to challenge the agency’s failure in court. The measure also converts the existing minimum public comment periods for CEQA documents into fixed maximums that can only be extended by court order – 20 days for an MND or negative declaration and 45 days for an EIR.
Many of these deadlines are not entirely new. Existing law already generally requires agencies to determine application completeness within 30 days and complete EIRs and MNDs within certain timelines. What BACA changes is that its deadlines run in business days rather than calendar days, apply to all essential project approvals — including legislative approvals such as general plan amendments and zone changes, which current deadlines do not reach — and, most significantly, are enforceable in court.
BACA Allows for a Streamlined Alternatives Analysis and Mandates Narrower Review of Project Impacts
In addition to the new deadlines, BACA allows essential project applicants to opt-in to a preliminary scoping process that once completed allows for a simplified project alternatives analysis. In place of CEQA’s standard requirement to study a “reasonable range” of project alternatives, the streamlined analysis need only address three options: the proposed project itself, a no-project alternative, and single on-site project alternative.
Notably, BACA requires public agencies to evaluate a project’s environmental impacts – including the significance of the impacts and potential ways to mitigate them – based on the project’s compliance with “existing laws.” Under BACA’s definition of existing laws, this restricts the agency in evaluating the project’s compliance with formally adopted written standards that existed and were in effect when the project application was submitted. This appears to be a significant change, because under CEQA as it exists today, an agency has substantial discretion to determine whether a project’s impacts are significant and may resort to many different sources of information in making those determinations, some of which might qualify as “existing laws” but many of which likely don’t. For example, currently, agencies can develop thresholds to determine whether a project’s impacts are significant on a project-by-project basis; and even if no written legal standards exist concerning a particular type of impact, agencies often rely on new scientific studies, new information raised in public comments, and agency standards developed after the project was submitted in defining project impacts. Under BACA, an agency’s discretion to formulate project-specific thresholds or to rely on non-objective or post-submittal information appears to be sharply curtailed, which may reduce the number of project impacts an agency may determine as significant in the course of the review process.
BACA Limits Judicial Review of Essential Projects
BACA also limits the scope of judicial review of essential project approvals. Opponents who challenge an approval of an essential project under BACA would be limited to challenging the approval on the grounds that the lead agency did not comply with existing laws and objective standards in place at the time the application was submitted. And regardless of the level of environmental review undertaken on an essential project – e.g., whether an EIR versus an MND was prepared – a court reviewing a challenge to a project approval is required to determine “only” whether the approval is supported by substantial evidence. This appears aimed at displacing the more petitioner-friendly “fair argument” standard that currently governs challenges to MNDs and negative declarations.
Finally, even if a court finds that an agency’s approval of an essential project was defective, the court may not rescind the entire approval. Instead, the court is limited to enjoining only the part of the development impacted by the agency’s non-compliance until it is corrected.
Looking Ahead to November
BACA will head to the November ballot with a significant financial and organizational head start, bolstered by a strong showing in initial polling. A public opinion poll released by the Public Policy Institute of California in July showed 73 percent of likely California voters supporting the measure. Some notable supporters of the measure include the California Building Industry Association, the California Hospital Association, NAACP California and Pacific Gas & Electric, and of course its sponsor, the California Chamber of Commerce. The measure has also attracted a notable Democratic endorsement from Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, the author of the Legislature’s landmark 2025 infill housing CEQA exemption. The Committee to Build an Affordable California, the CalChamber-led campaign committee, reported nearly $13.8 million in contributions through the first quarter of 2026 — including $10 million from Building a Better California, a committee funded largely by Silicon Valley donors, and $2 million from Edison International.
However, opposition is beginning to organize. The State Building and Construction Trades Council and the Sierra Club of California have announced their opposition. The lead opposition committee, One Voice for California, has raised over $4 million from the Trades Council and environmental advocacy organizations since the committee was opened last month. Notably, while several other initiatives were withdrawn from the November ballot in eleventh-hour deals with the Legislature and rival interest groups, no such compromise emerged on BACA.

The Problem

$75,000+ (https://yesonprop45.com/cost-of-delay-per-home/) added to every new home, which drives up rents and mortgages.
Billions added in taxpayer and consumer costs (https://yesonprop45.com/report-2026-09-25-economic-and-fiscal-impacts-of-proposition-45/) for hospitals, roads and clean energy projects.
Delayed progress on critical environmental projects to reduce pollution, prevent wildfires (https://www.latimes.com/environment/story/2025-11-25/cal-fire-approach-to-socals-wildfire-crisis-could-make-things-worse-court-says) and cut emissions.

Prop 45 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026) cuts red tape and unnecessary delays so California can build the essential infrastructure we need faster, lower our cost of living and improve our quality of life.
Including:
Clean water infrastructure
Clean Energy
Housing
Roads, bridges, and transit
Hospitals and health care facilities
Schools and educational facilities
Wildfire prevention
Broadband infrastructure
What Is Prop 45?
Proposition 45 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/analysis.htm), the Building an Affordable California Act (https://yesonprop45.com/read-the-measure/), is a 2026 California ballot proposition that modernizes the state's outdated approval process for essential projects like housing, water, clean energy, roads, schools and hospitals by setting enforceable timelines (https://yesonprop45.com/get-the-facts/) for agency decisions and court challenges, while keeping California's environmental, worker and tribal protections and local control (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publications/260730_2100_hb-letter-prop-45) in place.

Prop 45 will:
Reduce the cost of living
An analysis by the Blue Sky Consulting Group estimates Prop 45 would add nearly 20,000 homes a year (https://yesonprop45.com/report-2026-09-25-economic-and-fiscal-impacts-of-proposition-45/), or nearly 200,000 over ten years.
Accelerate the essential infrastructure California needs
Agencies must approve or deny project applications within 365 days (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026), and courts must resolve legal challenges within 270 days (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/analysis.htm).
Protect taxpayers by keeping public projects on time and on budget
The same analysis estimates $386 million a year in savings for public agencies (https://yesonprop45.com/report-2026-09-25-economic-and-fiscal-impacts-of-proposition-45/) on essential projects and $250 million a year for California ratepayers.
Create good-paying jobs and strengthen our economy
Projects built under Prop 45 must meet California's strongest-in-the-nation labor standards (https://yesonprop45.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Prop-45-Labor-Protections-Fact-Sheet-8.19.26.pdf), including fair pay and safe job sites.
Protect local control and community input
Local governments keep full authority (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publications/260730_2100_hb-letter-prop-45) to approve, deny or condition projects, and Prop 45 guarantees a 45-day public comment period with written responses to all timely comments.
Protect California's strong environmental, worker and tribal cultural protections
Prop 45 does not weaken or eliminate any environmental law (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publications/260730_2100_hb-letter-prop-45); CEQA (https://oag.ca.gov/environment/ceqa) remains fully in place.
Prop 45 speeds up approvals for the projects Californians rely on most:
Clean drinking water and supply projects
Hospitals, clinics and other health care facilities
Roads, bridges, transit and other transportation infrastructure
Wildfire prevention and resilience projects
Single and multi-family homes, senior and student housing
Clean energy generation, transmission and storage
Broadband and telecommunications infrastructure
Schools, classrooms and educational facilities

What does California Proposition 45 do?
Proposition 45 would overhaul the state’s landmark environmental review law, the California Environmental Quality Act. Sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce, the measure aims to help developers advance projects they designate as “essential” more quickly and easily. It would impose a 365-day limit on environmental reviews for those projects, including infrastructure like roads and bridges, housing, schools, broadband and wildfire mitigation. It would also require courts to rule within 270 days on lawsuits related to the environmental review law.

What do supporters and opponents say?
Supporters
Arguments for
The California Chamber of Commerce says the state’s environmental review law is outdated and allows for too much expensive bureaucracy and frivolous litigation that slows development. It argues that the delays ultimately increase costs that are passed down to taxpayers and consumers. The group argues the measure will speed up development while keeping essential environmental protections in place.
Supporter endorsements
California Chamber of Commerce
The California Hospital Association
California Children’s Hospital Association
California Primary Care Association
California Hydrogen Coalition
Agricultural Council of California
California Wind Energy Association
California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
California Council for Affordable Housing
California League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC)
California Housing Consortium
California Building Industry Association
Opponents
Arguments against
Opponents say the state’s environmental review law exists to protect people and the environment from potentially harmful developments. Weakening environmental review requirements, they say, would strip agencies of the tools they have to protect communities, increase costly litigation and practically eliminate their ability to enforce the law. They argue the long-term costs of poor planning will be passed onto agencies and taxpayers.
Opponent endorsements
Communities for a Better Environment
Beyond Plastics
Physicians for Social Responsibility- Los Angeles
Western Center on Law & Poverty
Californians Against Waste
Clean Water Action
Sierra Club California
Clean Air Coalition
Learning Disabilities Association of California
California Nurses for Environmental Health and Justice
Center for Food Safety
California Democratic Party (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf)
Ballot text
This is how the proposition will appear on the ballot.
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE. Amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects (including most housing, transportation, water, and health projects) by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Fiscal Impact: Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars potentially exceeding $100 million–annually, partly covered by fees. Uncertain, potentially more significant positive or negative longer-term fiscal effects.
Source: California Secretary of State (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/public-display)

An update and analysis of the most significant CEQA reform in 50+ years.
January 22, 2026
On December 26, 2005, the California Chamber of Commerce received an official Title & Summary (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/Title%20and%20Summary%20%2825-0023A1%29.pdf) from the Attorney General’s office for the Building an Affordable California Act (https://buildaffordableca.com/) (referred to here as the “Affordable CA”), and began signature gathering the first week of January. Early response has been strong—California voters are eager to sign a petition that cuts delays and lowers the cost of housing, electricity, and other everyday necessities. The Chamber is well on its way to qualifying Affordable CA for the November 2026 ballot, with signature collection on track to conclude by mid-April.
Based on our combined decades of experience advising, entitling, litigating, and defending projects subject to the California Environmental Quality Act (“CEQA”) throughout California, we have reviewed Affordable CA from a legal, procedural, and implementation perspective. Our analysis reflects extensive, first-hand experience with CEQA compliance, agency review, administrative records, and judicial review at every stage of project development.
Affordable CA represents the most comprehensive and consequential CEQA reform in more than 50 years. It eliminates open-ended delays by imposing enforceable timelines on all reviewing agencies, creates predictability in permitting processes through reliance on objective standards and vested rights, and curbs abusive litigation practices that delay projects without environmental benefit. Unlike prior CEQA reforms, which relied on narrow exemptions or project-specific streamlining, Affordable CA delivers systemwide, enforceable process reforms across eight essential project categories.
Based on our analysis, we conclude that the Building an Affordable California Act is legally sound, carefully calibrated, and extraordinarily effective. If enacted, it would materially reduce approval timelines and litigation risk for essential projects — often by multiple years — while preserving meaningful environmental review, public participation, and strong worker and tribal protections.
Core Reforms & Essential Projects
Affordable CA applies its reforms to a defined set of essential projects central to California’s affordability, climate, and public safety goals, including:
Housing : New single-family homes, apartments, senior and student housing, supportive and farmworker housing, and conversion of commercial buildings for residential use.
Public Health : Hospitals, community clinics, and medical office facilities that expand access to care.
Clean Energy : Solar, wind, geothermal, clean hydrogen, battery storage, fuel cells, clean carbon capture, upgrades to the electric grid, transmission lines, and EV charging networks.
Water Infrastructure : Water-quality treatment, groundwater recharge, water recycling and desalination plants, dams, stormwater capture, and other projects that deliver safe drinking water and strengthen California’s drought resilience.
Education Facilities : K–12 schools, community colleges, public and private nonprofit colleges and universities, including CSU/UC campuses, labs, and student support facilities.
Public Safety & Wildfire Resilience : Fire and police stations, vegetation management, undergrounding utilities, home hardening, and fuel break maintenance.
Transportation : Road repairs, bridges, public transit expansions, bike and pedestrian safety projects, and electric vehicle infrastructure.
Broadband & Digital Access : Fiber-optic and wireless broadband projects connecting underserved and rural communities.
Importantly, Affordable CA applies not only to the primary project, but also to the ancillary infrastructure required to place the project into service, including access roads, interconnections, sewage systems, pipelines, substations, etc. This ensures streamlining applies to the entire project delivery pathway, rather than allowing projects to be stalled through separate, sequential approvals.
Streamlined Approvals
1. Enforceable Timelines Across the Entire Approval Process
For the first time, CEQA timelines are mandatory and enforceable from application submittal through final approval for all types of CEQA documents.
Application Completeness . Agencies have 30 days to determine completeness or the application is deemed complete by operation of law. Any incompleteness notice must include a single , exhaustive list of missing items. Applicants have 90 days to cure identified deficiencies, then agencies receive an additional 30-day review period for any resubmittals. Any incompleteness finding may be appealed and must be resolved within 60 days . These requirements eliminate serial information requests and prolonged front-end delays.
CEQA Review Timelines . Once an application is complete, agencies must select the appropriate CEQA pathway within 30 days and complete environmental review within fixed deadlines:
90 days for exemptions and addenda
180 days for NDs/MNDs
365 days for EIRs
If an agency misses a deadline, the applicant may force a public hearing requiring final action within 60 days.
Concurrent and Coordinated Permitting. Once CEQA review is complete, all other permits, authorizations and approvals required for the same project by other agencies must be issued within 90 days of application completeness or, for exempt projects, within 90 days of the exemption determination . This prevents sequential permitting delays after CEQA compliance has been achieved.
Phased Approvals. Components of a qualifying larger project may proceed independently under Affordable CA timelines, allowing essential projects to advance in phases even if individual phases would not qualify on their own.
Preserves Lead Agency Decision Authority . Importantly, while Affordable CA enforces strict timelines it does not force project approvals. State and local agencies retain full authority to approve, reject and condition projects.
2. Vested Rights
Affordable CA restores predictability by requiring agencies to evaluate projects based solely on the laws, regulations and written standards in effect at the time of application submittal, including statutes, regulations, ordinances, and routinely applied thresholds of significance. This prevents midstream policy shifts or unwritten expectations from derailing pending projects. Applicants may voluntarily waive vested rights if they elect to proceed under newer standards.
3. Streamlined Alternatives Analysis
Affordable CA narrows the required alternatives analysis under CEQA to:
One applicant-proposed feasible alternative
The required “no project” alternative
The measure establishes a presumption that the applicant-proposed alternative satisfies CEQA’s feasibility requirement. This reform addresses one of the most common sources of delay, expanded administrative records, and litigation risk, often driven by demands to evaluate speculative alternatives that are not economically, technically, or legally feasible.
4. Firm Public Comment Periods
Affordable CA provides clear, enforceable public comment timelines:
20-day public comment period for NDs and MNDs
45-day public comment period for EIRs
Late comments are excluded except in limited circumstances involving information that could not reasonably have been raised earlier. Rights to comment at public hearings, even those after the comment period, are preserved. Continued hearings must be set to a date certain and do not reopen comment periods, preserving meaningful public participation while preventing procedural gamesmanship.
Faster, Fairer and More Predictable Judicial Review
1. Judicial Review Shot Clock
CEQA challenges must be filed within 30 days of the notice of determination or exemption . Courts must resolve CEQA challenges, including appeals, within 270 days , subject to a 90-day extension.
2. Severance – Only Fix What’s Broken
Affordable CA replaces CEQA’s all-or-nothing remedy structure. If a court identifies a flaw in one portion of a CEQA document, it may require correction of only that issue while allowing legally compliant portions of the project to proceed on schedule.
3. Objective Standards for Judicial Review
Courts may only overturn a project approval if the lead agency failed to comply with objective, written standards in effect at the time of application submittal. Subjective criteria or unpublished standards may not be used to invalidate approvals.
4. Substantial Evidence Standard
All CEQA documents must be upheld where supported by substantial evidence in the record.
Maintains California’s Strong Environmental, Tribal & Labor Protections
Affordable CA does not exempt projects from CEQA or from compliance with any other state or federal environmental law, and all substantive environmental protections remain fully intact, including the Clean Water Act, Clean Air Act, Endangered Species Act, and California Coastal Act. The measure preserves and strengthens tribal consultation under Assembly Bill 52 by requiring earlier engagement and incorporating Tribal Traditional Knowledge into the consultation process. Affordable CA also maintains California’s strongest labor standards, including AB 130 requirements for essential housing projects and Environmental Leadership Development Project-level labor standards for all other essential projects.
Bottom Line
Affordable CA fundamentally changes the risk profile of building in California by imposing enforceable timelines, objective review standards, and predictable judicial remedies. Based on our experience, we believe Affordable CA will cut years — not months — from project timelines, reduce carrying costs and enable California to deliver housing, infrastructure and essential services at scale without sacrificing environmental integrity or worker protections .
The Building an Affordable California Act represents a once-in-a-generation opportunity to realign CEQA with its intended purpose. We believe the measure is legally sound, carefully drafted, and urgently needed, and we encourage serious engagement with this effort, including consideration of support for its placement and passage on the November 2026 ballot.

Summary of California Chamber of Commerce Initiative
to Amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA)
Overview
The California Chamber of Commerce is propounding a statewide ballot initiative that
significantly rolls back environmental protections guaranteed by the California Environmental
Quality Act (CEQA). Officially titled “Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects,” the
Initiative weakens environmental review requirements for a broad range of projects, including
major infrastructure developments, to the benefit of developers. It also limits the ability of
communities to advocate for necessary public health protections, exposes public agencies to
increased liability risks, and strips courts of the power to issue a meaningful remedy when
CEQA is violated.
“Essential” Projects Covered by the Initiative
The Initiative applies to eight categories of projects, each labeled “essential”: housing, energy
infrastructure, water infrastructure, public health, public safety, transportation, educational
facilities, and broadband internet.
Each category encompasses a broad range of project types. Some of the most consequential
include:
• Major transportation infrastructure projects, including highways, bridges, interchanges,
tunnels, and ferry terminals;
• Major energy projects, including municipal solid waste conversion projects, landfill gas
facilities, dairy biogas projects, and electrical transmission systems and infrastructure;
• Major water infrastructure projects, including dams, reservoirs, canals, desalination
plants, and other water system components;
• Residential and specified mixed-use projects located anywhere in the state, including
large-scale developments in fire-prone sprawl areas; and
• Wildfire risk reduction projects, including vegetation management and fuel reduction
(potentially including forest clear-cutting).
The Initiative also covers all ancillary infrastructure components included in the qualifying
project’s application as part of the “whole of the project.” These ancillary components could
include, for example, wastewater treatment centers (ancillary to geothermal sites and water
systems) or major gas pipelines (ancillary to landfill gas energy projects).
The Initiative does not apply to new oil or natural gas production facilities, the Delta
Conveyance Project, nuclear facilities, high-speed rail systems, or jails and other detention
facilities.
2
Initiative’s New Rules for “Essential” Projects
1. Eliminates Longstanding Principle Favoring Environmental Protection
The Initiative states that its language should be interpreted and implemented to “afford the fullest
possible weight to the interest of, and the approval and realization of, essential projects.” This
reverses CEQA’s bedrock principle that the law must be interpreted to afford the fullest possible
protection of the environment.
2. Makes Procedural Changes
The Initiative provides new procedural requirements that restrict environmental review,
including but not limited to the following:
• It tightly limits the duration of public comment periods for most environmental
documents and provides that these comment periods can be extended only by court order
(an exception to this limitation exists where the lead agency is also the project applicant).
As a result, comment deadlines will become unreasonable for many projects. The new
rules specify:
o A maximum of 20 days for comments on negative declarations and mitigated
negative declarations (rather than a minimum of 20 days, or 30 days if state
agency review is required, as current law provides).
o A maximum of 45 days for comments on environmental impact reports (EIRs)
(rather than a minimum of 30 days, or 45 days if state agency review is required,
as current law provides).
Note: Comment periods are the principal opportunity for regulatory agencies and the
public to request information about a proposed project and to suggest mitigation
measures. Commenting agencies include “trustee agencies,” which must comment on a
proposed project’s effect on wildlife and other resources, and “responsible agencies,”
which have permit authority over projects. The new maximum time periods will reduce
the public’s and agencies’ ability to provide informed feedback and seek vital
information.
• It greatly expands the number and types of development projects subject to the strict
requirement that agencies determine the completeness of development applications
within 30 days. If a determination is not granted within that period, the application is
automatically deemed complete, limiting information that agencies can require of the
applicant in the future.
• It requires responsible agencies to act on project applications within 90 days of a
complete application, or within 1 day after the lead agency approves the project,
whichever date is later. This could make it more difficult for responsible agencies to
ensure that environmental documents prepared by lead agencies are sufficient for their
purposes, which could delay the issuance of necessary environmental permits.
3
• It eliminates the requirement for consultation with California Native American tribes that
are not federally recognized.
• It allows qualifying projects that are currently in the approval pipeline to take advantage
of the new relaxed rules. Applications can be withdrawn and resubmitted. Relatedly, it
provides that all projects deemed complete prior to the Initiative’s effective date shall
remain complete, even if the applicant has significantly altered the project since
submitting its application.
3. Allows Developers to Sue Public Agencies Under CEQA
The Initiative would create a new right of action for applicants to sue public agencies that deny
their projects. This represents a major change in the law that could significantly increase
litigation under CEQA, cost public agencies more in attorney fees, and pressure them to issue
project approvals even when the project might harm local communities and the environment.
Except for specified housing projects, CEQA does not currently allow applicants to sue over
project denials.
4. Weakens Standards for Environmental Review
Background: Under current law, CEQA requires that lead agencies determine whether a
proposed project’s environmental impacts are “significant.” If the lead agency concludes the
project will cause a significant impact, CEQA mandates that it adopt mitigation measures to
reduce that impact to a level of insignificance. Notably, CEQA requires agencies to use
“thresholds of significance” that are based on up-to-date scientific information and designed to
uncover the actual harm that a proposed project will cause.
What does the Initiative do?
The Initiative requires that the lead agency determine a proposed project’s significant impacts
based solely on compliance with “existing laws.”
• “Existing laws” mean formally adopted legal requirements in statutes, regulations, rules,
standards, or ordinances that were in effect when the application was submitted. The
Initiative does not require that these laws/standards be designed to disclose significant
harm to the environment.
• The Initiative creates narrow exceptions, allowing an agency to base its significance
determination on updated building codes and laws addressing “life-safety” impacts that
were enacted after an application was submitted.
• If the lead agency has employed thresholds of significance on the earlier of the date an
applicant’s preapplication or application is filed, the applicant may elect to “vest into”
any of those thresholds.
The Initiative’s new rules for significance determinations represent a major change in CEQA.
• By allowing thresholds of significance to be based on any existing laws, including laws
that may not adequately protect the public or the environment, or that may not be based
on current or accurate scientific knowledge, the Initiative undermines CEQA’s core
purpose: to identify, disclose, and mitigate significant impacts.
4
• Allowing applicants to choose the applicable thresholds of significance reverses current
law, which gives the lead agency sole authority over the analysis of environmental
impacts.
5. Allows Abbreviated Alternatives Analysis
Background: Under current law, CEQA requires that an EIR include a reasonable range of
feasible alternatives that are less harmful to the environment than the proposed project. Further,
the alternatives analysis must consider alternative locations if necessary to reduce the project’s
significant impacts; indeed, the project location is often one of the major factors contributing to
harm to the environment and public health. Finally, lead agencies must consider and formally
respond to feasible alternative proposals received in public comments.
What does the Initiative do?
The Initiative provides an optional pathway, or preliminary scoping process, that allows
applicants to include only one project alternative (in addition to the “no project” alternative) in
the EIR. It thus eliminates the requirement that the analysis include a range of options. In
addition, it removes the requirement that the agency consider alternative locations if necessary.
Further, for applicants electing the preliminary scoping process, lead agencies are barred from
considering environmentally superior alternatives proposed by the public.
This new rule is a major change in CEQA. The requirement under current law that the lead
agency identify a range of less harmful alternatives (including alternative sites) and consider
options proposed by the public goes to the heart of CEQA – this is how the law improves
projects that would otherwise damage communities or the environment.
6. Makes Changes to Judicial Review and Limits Remedy in CEQA Cases
Through several key changes, the Initiative limits judicial review and remedies in CEQA cases
challenging qualifying projects.
a. Rushes Judicial Review
Background: For most projects, current law does not impose a time limit for completing CEQA
litigation. A notable exception applies to developments identified as “Leadership” projects under
CEQA and clean energy projects under the California Energy Commission’s Opt-In Certification
Program, for which legal challenges must be completed within 270 days (including trial and
appellate courts), if feasible. The “Leadership” project pathway requires applicants to reimburse
for additional costs incurred by the courts in complying with the expedited timelines.
What does the Initiative do?
The Initiative provides that any CEQA case challenging a qualifying project must be completed
within 270 days (including all trial and appellate court proceedings). The court may, at its
discretion, extend the deadline by 90 days, but any further extension requires the consent of the
petitioner, the agency, and the applicant. The Initiative thus appears to remove the court’s
discretion to extend the deadline beyond 360 days even if it is infeasible to complete all judicial
proceedings within the specified time frame.
The Initiative does not require that applicants reimburse for the burden the expedited process will
place on the courts.
5
b. Changes Standard of Review
Background: Under current law, CEQA provides a dual standard of judicial review:
• If the court is deciding a legal question, the “de novo” standard applies. Here, the court
exercises its independent judgment and does not defer to the lead agency’s decision.
o Example 1 of legal question: whether the EIR’s analysis of project impacts
omitted information necessary to the agency’s informed decision-making.
o Example 2 of legal question: whether the agency complied with CEQA’s
procedural requirements. Notably, where an agency is found to have committed a
procedural error, the error is presumptively prejudicial.
• If the court is deciding a factual question, the “substantial evidence test” applies. Here,
the agency’s decision must be upheld if it is supported by substantial evidence in the
record. Under these circumstances, the court must defer to the agency’s determination,
even if contrary evidence exists to support the petitioner’s argument.
o Example of factual question: whether the lead agency based its conclusions about
air quality impacts on incorrect modeling.
What does the Initiative do?
First, the Initiative provides that petitioners’ claims are limited to whether the lead agency failed
to comply with “objective existing laws.”
• “Objective” means “involving no personal or subjective judgment and being uniformly
verifiable by reference to an external and uniform benchmark or criterion available and
knowable by both the applicant and the public agency before the application was
submitted.”
• “Existing laws” is defined above (see #4).
This new requirement reduces CEQA’s protections considerably, because not all “objective
existing laws” will capture the full extent of a project’s impacts or ensure effective mitigation of
its impacts.
Second, the Initiative provides that, with one exception (described below), all claims must be
decided under the “substantial evidence test.” Under this standard, the court must defer to the
agency’s CEQA determinations, rather than exercising its independent judgment.
• This is a major change in the law. The “substantial evidence test” has never been applied
in cases where a court is deciding purely legal questions, such as whether an EIR omitted
crucial analysis. In fact, because the existing “independent judgment” standard applies to
legal questions throughout all areas of state and local agency decision-making, the
Initiative’s change would purport to change the standard of review uniquely for CEQA
cases.
6
Third, the Initiative provides that for any claim alleging that the lead agency did not complete
CEQA’s “public participation procedures,” the court must determine only whether the agency’s
failure was “arbitrary and capricious and resulted in prejudicial error.”
• This is another major limitation to judicial discretion. Courts currently exercise their
independent judgment to decide these procedural claims and do not employ the
deferential “arbitrary and capricious standard.” In addition, the Initiative eliminates the
presumption that procedural errors are prejudicial. Finally, the Initiative does not define
“public participation procedures,” an ambiguous term.
7. Curtails Remedies that Courts May Issue
Background: Under current law, if a court finds that the lead agency has violated CEQA, the
standard remedy where there is clear demonstration of harm is to direct the agency to rescind the
project approval. The court typically will also enjoin the project’s construction until the agency
demonstrates to the court that the CEQA error has been corrected. CEQA allows courts to limit
the injunction to a specific part or activity of the project, but only if that discrete part or activity
can be severed from the rest of the project and such severance will not prejudice complete and
full compliance with CEQA.
What does the Initiative do?
The Initiative curtails the remedy a court can issue, in three fundamental ways.
First, a court would not be able to order rescission of an agency’s approval of a qualifying
project even if it finds an egregious violation of CEQA. This provision would thus allow a
permitting decision to remain in place despite being based on incorrect or incomplete
information.
Second, a court would only be able to prohibit the commencement of the specific part or activity
of the project that is affected by the CEQA error. Unlike current law, the Initiative appears to
allow such severance of project activities even where it might prejudice complete and full
compliance with CEQA.
Third, a court would be limited to issuing a “temporary” injunction only where there is clear and
convincing evidence that the project would have a “specific, adverse impact upon public safety.”
Thus, a court cannot enjoin activities that would degrade water or air quality, destroy habitat for
endangered species, or pose risks to public health.
• Any injunction is limited to temporarily halting the “particular essential project
component that would result in the specific, adverse impact upon public safety.” The
proponents do not reference any law in California that prevents a court from issuing a
permanent injunction when appropriate.
• To obtain an injunction, the petitioner must show that there is no feasible way to mitigate
or avoid the adverse impact on public safety.
• The Initiative is unclear whether these restrictions on injunctions would apply to its
provision allowing a court to prohibit the commencement of a project after the court has
found a CEQA violation.
7
Fourth, the Initiative provides that any phase of a challenged project that is not within the scope
of the CEQA error identified by the court may not be subject to the writ or any further challenge.
In addition, if the agency’s project approval was not challenged, the Initiative disallows any
CEQA challenge to later project actions and approvals. This represents a major change to CEQA,
which does not preclude further litigation to enforce compliance with CEQA for each phase of
the project. For example, under current law, petitioners can file a CEQA action if the developer
fails to implement required mitigation of significant project impacts.
8. Limits Contents of the Administrative Record
Background: Courts review claims of CEQA violation by examining the “administrative record”
of information the agency considered when it decided to approve a project. Current law requires
that administrative records include a broad range of documents in the lead agency’s possession
that relate to the challenged project. These documents include comments on the agency’s
environmental review, which can be submitted at any time before the close of the public hearing
to approve the project. Because discovery is precluded in CEQA litigation, the administrative
record is generally the only evidence on which a court evaluates a case. It offers important
insights into how the lead agency determined the project’s significant impacts and identified
measures to avoid or mitigate those impacts.
What does the Initiative do?
The Initiative provides radical new limitations on the contents of administrative records.
First, administrative records may consist only of notices, studies and documents that are required
under CEQA to be sent or distributed to members of the public by the lead agency, or made
available to the public at a public repository or on the agency’s website.
• Under this new rule, the record would not include internal agency communications,
project applications, or agency communications with applicants, along with many other
types of documents that may provide insight into a project’s impacts, as required by
current law.
Second, public comments in the administrative record are generally limited to (a) electronic and
written comments received during comment periods on environmental documents; (b) electronic
and written comments received 48+ hours before hearings, subject to strict limitations described
below; and (c) verbal testimony at noticed recorded hearings. However, the record shall include,
“without qualification,” responses by the lead agency or the applicant to comments, or comments
from the applicant in response to a question from an agency or to demonstrate compliance with
CEQA.
• Electronic/written comments from the public received 48+ hours before a public hearing,
but not submitted during the comment period, may be included in the administrative

o A “significant change” to the project precluded the comment from being raised

CEQA Reform Qualifies for the Ballot: What to Know About the Building an Affordable California Act
July 15, 2026 - E-Alerts (https://www.rutan.com/category/e-alerts/)

On June 25, 2026, the Building an Affordable California Act (“BACA”), a statewide measure sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce, officially qualified for the November 2026 General Election ballot. The initiative will appear on California ballots this November as Prop 45. If passed by voters, BACA would reform the California Environmental Quality Act (“CEQA”) to create a broad category of “essential projects” that are entitled to a narrower environmental review process, the option to engage in a streamlined project alternatives analysis and more limited judicial review in the event of a project challenge. Early polling shows BACA garnering significant support among California voters, with 73 percent of likely voters indicating their support for the measure in a recently released poll.
BACA Streamlines Environmental Review for Essential Projects
BACA applies only to developments that qualify as “essential projects.” Specifically included are “essential housing projects,” which the law defines as housing projects including residential units only, residential mixed-use projects, commercial-to-residential conversions, subdivisions consisting of residential units or unimproved residential lots, and a number of specific housing categories including transitional housing, student housing, and senior housing. Other types of essential projects include qualifying water, clean energy, public health, public safety, broadband Internet access, education facility, and transportation projects. Essential projects utilizing BACA’s CEQA review provisions, except for housing projects under 85 feet above grade, must pay prevailing wages to all construction workers.
BACA would modify certain procedures and time limits for environmental review of essential projects. First, agencies will have 30 days to determine whether an essential project application is complete. If the agency fails to meet the completeness deadline, then the essential project application will automatically be deemed complete.
Once an agency has determined whether the project will require an Environmental Impact Report (“EIR”), Mitigated Negative Declaration (“MND”) or negative declaration, or than an exemption applies, the measure imposes various deadlines for the agency to make a final determination, which run from the date the application is deemed complete: 365 business days to certify an EIR, 180 business days to adopt a negative declaration, and 90 business days to make a final exemption determination. If the agency fails to meet these deadlines in making a final determination, the applicant has the option of requesting a meeting or hearing, which the agency would be required to hold within 60 days and either approve or deny the project at the meeting, and thereafter maintains an express right to challenge the agency’s failure in court. The measure also converts the existing minimum public comment periods for CEQA documents into fixed maximums that can only be extended by court order – 20 days for an MND or negative declaration and 45 days for an EIR.
Many of these deadlines are not entirely new. Existing law already generally requires agencies to determine application completeness within 30 days and complete EIRs and MNDs within certain timelines. What BACA changes is that its deadlines run in business days rather than calendar days, apply to all essential project approvals — including legislative approvals such as general plan amendments and zone changes, which current deadlines do not reach — and, most significantly, are enforceable in court.
BACA Allows for a Streamlined Alternatives Analysis and Mandates Narrower Review of Project Impacts
In addition to the new deadlines, BACA allows essential project applicants to opt-in to a preliminary scoping process that once completed allows for a simplified project alternatives analysis. In place of CEQA’s standard requirement to study a “reasonable range” of project alternatives, the streamlined analysis need only address three options: the proposed project itself, a no-project alternative, and single on-site project alternative.
Notably, BACA requires public agencies to evaluate a project’s environmental impacts – including the significance of the impacts and potential ways to mitigate them – based on the project’s compliance with “existing laws.” Under BACA’s definition of existing laws, this restricts the agency in evaluating the project’s compliance with formally adopted written standards that existed and were in effect when the project application was submitted. This appears to be a significant change, because under CEQA as it exists today, an agency has substantial discretion to determine whether a project’s impacts are significant and may resort to many different sources of information in making those determinations, some of which might qualify as “existing laws” but many of which likely don’t. For example, currently, agencies can develop thresholds to determine whether a project’s impacts are significant on a project-by-project basis; and even if no written legal standards exist concerning a particular type of impact, agencies often rely on new scientific studies, new information raised in public comments, and agency standards developed after the project was submitted in defining project impacts. Under BACA, an agency’s discretion to formulate project-specific thresholds or to rely on non-objective or post-submittal information appears to be sharply curtailed, which may reduce the number of project impacts an agency may determine as significant in the course of the review process.
BACA Limits Judicial Review of Essential Projects
BACA also limits the scope of judicial review of essential project approvals. Opponents who challenge an approval of an essential project under BACA would be limited to challenging the approval on the grounds that the lead agency did not comply with existing laws and objective standards in place at the time the application was submitted. And regardless of the level of environmental review undertaken on an essential project – e.g., whether an EIR versus an MND was prepared – a court reviewing a challenge to a project approval is required to determine “only” whether the approval is supported by substantial evidence. This appears aimed at displacing the more petitioner-friendly “fair argument” standard that currently governs challenges to MNDs and negative declarations.
Finally, even if a court finds that an agency’s approval of an essential project was defective, the court may not rescind the entire approval. Instead, the court is limited to enjoining only the part of the development impacted by the agency’s non-compliance until it is corrected.
Looking Ahead to November
BACA will head to the November ballot with a significant financial and organizational head start, bolstered by a strong showing in initial polling. A public opinion poll released by the Public Policy Institute of California in July showed 73 percent of likely California voters supporting the measure. Some notable supporters of the measure include the California Building Industry Association, the California Hospital Association, NAACP California and Pacific Gas & Electric, and of course its sponsor, the California Chamber of Commerce. The measure has also attracted a notable Democratic endorsement from Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, the author of the Legislature’s landmark 2025 infill housing CEQA exemption. The Committee to Build an Affordable California, the CalChamber-led campaign committee, reported nearly $13.8 million in contributions through the first quarter of 2026 — including $10 million from Building a Better California, a committee funded largely by Silicon Valley donors, and $2 million from Edison International.
However, opposition is beginning to organize. The State Building and Construction Trades Council and the Sierra Club of California have announced their opposition. The lead opposition committee, One Voice for California, has raised over $4 million from the Trades Council and environmental advocacy organizations since the committee was opened last month. Notably, while several other initiatives were withdrawn from the November ballot in eleventh-hour deals with the Legislature and rival interest groups, no such compromise emerged on BACA.

What Is Prop 45?
Proposition 45 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/analysis.htm), the Building an Affordable California Act (https://yesonprop45.com/read-the-measure/), is a 2026 California ballot proposition that modernizes the state's outdated approval process for essential projects like housing, water, clean energy, roads, schools and hospitals by setting enforceable timelines (https://yesonprop45.com/get-the-facts/) for agency decisions and court challenges, while keeping California's environmental, worker and tribal protections and local control (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publications/260730_2100_hb-letter-prop-45) in place.

Prop 45 will:
Reduce the cost of living
An analysis by the Blue Sky Consulting Group estimates Prop 45 would add nearly 20,000 homes a year (https://yesonprop45.com/report-2026-09-25-economic-and-fiscal-impacts-of-proposition-45/), or nearly 200,000 over ten years.
Accelerate the essential infrastructure California needs
Agencies must approve or deny project applications within 365 days (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026), and courts must resolve legal challenges within 270 days (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/analysis.htm).
Protect taxpayers by keeping public projects on time and on budget
The same analysis estimates $386 million a year in savings for public agencies (https://yesonprop45.com/report-2026-09-25-economic-and-fiscal-impacts-of-proposition-45/) on essential projects and $250 million a year for California ratepayers.
Create good-paying jobs and strengthen our economy
Projects built under Prop 45 must meet California's strongest-in-the-nation labor standards (https://yesonprop45.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Prop-45-Labor-Protections-Fact-Sheet-8.19.26.pdf), including fair pay and safe job sites.
Protect local control and community input
Local governments keep full authority (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publications/260730_2100_hb-letter-prop-45) to approve, deny or condition projects, and Prop 45 guarantees a 45-day public comment period with written responses to all timely comments.
Protect California's strong environmental, worker and tribal cultural protections
Prop 45 does not weaken or eliminate any environmental law (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publications/260730_2100_hb-letter-prop-45); CEQA (https://oag.ca.gov/environment/ceqa) remains fully in place.
Prop 45 speeds up approvals for the projects Californians rely on most:
Clean drinking water and supply projects
Hospitals, clinics and other health care facilities
Roads, bridges, transit and other transportation infrastructure
Wildfire prevention and resilience projects
Single and multi-family homes, senior and student housing
Clean energy generation, transmission and storage
Broadband and telecommunications infrastructure
Schools, classrooms and educational facilities

it looks very different from the draft (there is no formal comment
period on a final environmental document).
The Initiative’s restrictions on the contents of administrative records limit decision-making
transparency, a key objective of CEQA, and mean that in situations where, for example, agency
staff express doubts about the integrity of information contained in CEQA documents or
provided by project applicants, that information will not ordinarily be part of the record. The
Initiative’s limitations on public comments on environmental documents – limitations that do not
apply to the applicant – discourage public participation in the environmental review process,
another hallmark of CEQA. Overall, these restrictions on the administrative record give the
views of the applicant and agency more weight than those of the public, and will undermine
petitioners’ ability to successfully prosecute CEQA claims.
General Provisions
The Initiative has a number of “general” provisions, addressing subjects like severability,
effective date, and statutory references. While most of these provisions are typical for statewide
initiatives, one stands out as unusual and over-reaching.
Defense of Initiative in Event of Legal Challenge
If the Initiative is subject to legal challenge and the Attorney General and the Governor refuse to
defend it, the Attorney General must appoint independent outside counsel to do so. In this
circumstance, a “continuous appropriation” will be made from the General Fund to the
Controller, without regard to fiscal years, in an amount necessary to cover the costs of retaining
independent counsel. This appears to be highly unusual and may expose the state to substantial
financial liability.
