Δ
Public agencies are responsible for comparing the effects of a range of project alternatives, including a “no project” scenario.
Agencies judge project impacts using environmental standards they choose, covering everything from noise to air pollution, and they can revise those standards as new information emerges.
The public can then submit comments and suggest project alternatives, which the lead agency must consider. Members of the public, environmental groups and other stakeholders can sue to challenge reviews they think are illegal or incomplete.
Prop. 45 would give agencies 365 business days to decide on an environmental impact report for projects the measure defines as essential, including housing, roads, water, broadband and wildfire mitigation, and require courts to resolve cases within 270 calendar days.
Eligible applicants could choose the new procedures or stay with the existing ones.
What supporters and opponents say
Supporters of Prop. 45 say that the current process causes unnecessary delays and expenses, (https://www.hklaw.com/-/media/files/insights/publications/2026/09/hernandez_2026ceqastudy.pdf) including the costs of reviewing late public comments and defending against litigation.
Jennifer Barrera, chief executive of the California Chamber of Commerce, said the delays are costly.
“Time is money, and the delays that we see with regards to all of the red tape and bureaucracy … it could be anywhere from six to 10 years added on to the determination of moving a project forward,” Barrera said. “All those costs are ultimately borne by the consumers.”
Dan Dunmoyer, chief executive of the California Building Industry Association, said the proposition would decrease the cost of the average home by $75,000.
“If we want to have a society where people can live and thrive, we’ve got to find the sweet spot, and we think Prop. 45 is the sweet spot,” Dunmoyer said.
Opponents — a coalition that includes environmental groups, some labor unions and the California Democratic Party — say the measure goes far beyond basic streamlining, and gives project applicants too much power, undercutting the point of CEQA. They say Prop. 45 would strip agencies of the tools they have to protect communities, increase costly litigation and practically eliminate agencies’ ability to enforce the law.
“When you’re undoing or undermining environmental review, or saying you don’t need to do as much environmental review, you can have less community input for a project,” said Aruna Prabhala, an attorney for the Center for Biological Diversity who works on the opposition campaign.
A power shift?
Prop. 45 doesn’t just make the process go faster. It also changes (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026) the rules for project applicants and the government agencies overseeing the review process, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the Legislature’s nonpartisan adviser.
Applicants could choose just one project alternative for the agency to consider rather than the multiple alternatives agencies assess today. Agencies would have to judge a project’s impacts under the standards in place when the applicant applies, rather than revising them as new information emerges, and list everything an application requires up front. If an agency misses the 365-business-day deadline, the applicant could request a hearing and potentially sue.
The public and courts would have less say. Public comments would be subject to a strict 45-day deadline, and any late comments can’t be entered into the record that a judge could review if there’s litigation.
Courts could still order agencies to fix flawed reviews, but could stop only the part of a project that failed to comply, not the whole project.
Traffic flows past construction work on eastbound Highway 50 in Sacramento on Aug. 12, 2021. Photo by Rich Pedroncelli, AP Photo
The same rules would apply when public agencies are developers themselves. Agencies building roads or water systems, for instance, would have the option of just analyzing one project alternative and choosing the environmental rules that apply at the time of submission. If they’re sued and a court finds they made a mistake with just one piece of their review, the overall project could still move forward.
Sean Marciniak, an attorney for Hanson Bridgett, which helped the California Chamber of Commerce write the measure, said agencies would keep the power to reject projects and the measure would not override other planning or zoning laws.
“This will protect agencies in their decisions,” he said.
Why a county group is sitting this out
Organizations that represent local governments in California, including the League of California Cities and the California State Association of Counties, have mostly stayed out of the debate.
California’s rural counties say they have a problem with building housing, and they’ve historically advocated for CEQA reform.
These counties often have small populations. They’re strapped for cash and the staff needed to handle the complicated process, said John Kennedy, a policy advocate for the Rural County Representatives of California.
So when the California Chamber of Commerce proposed a ballot initiative to speed up environmental reviews, Prop. 45 at first looked like a natural fit.
“CEQA has long been misused and manipulated by a number of interest groups seeking to extract their own interests,” Kennedy said.
But the group, which represents parts of 40 counties, is sitting this one out. Its leaders voted to stay neutral; Kennedy said he suggested the group oppose it because he thinks it goes too far.
“Prop. 45 really puts the power in the hands of the project proponents, project developers, and limits local authority to require consideration of alternatives,” he said.
He worries local agencies would lose control over the standards that decide when noise, dust or runoff is significant enough to require action.
What Prop. 45 would have changed
In Richardson Grove, had the Caltrans case come up after Prop. 45, Caltrans could have benefited from a 270-calendar-day time limit on courts to resolve the case. If a court found a flaw, it could stop only the part of the project that fell short.
The case, Marciniak said, also shows how Caltrans could have used existing standards to make the review go more smoothly and quickly. In 2014, an appeals court found Caltrans’ environmental report applied no standard for judging harm to the redwoods’ roots, and noted a state parks handbook with guidelines for protecting trees from construction damage. “There are easy tweaks any agency can make to crystallize meaningful thresholds of significance,” he said.
Opponents say the case is not typical. It’s rare for a case to take so long, said Doug Carstens, an attorney who often represents environmental groups in CEQA cases. The fixes courts required made the review better, he added.
“In this instance you’re talking about trees, but Prop. 45 could also apply to an instance where there’s people,” Carstens said. “It’s a question of going too far.”
What would it cost, and what would it save
New housing construction in the Crocker Village neighborhood in Sacramento on Feb. 10, 2022. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters
The measure’s backers pitch it as an answer to California’s cost-of-living crisis.
Amelia Matier, a spokesperson for the Prop. 45 campaign, said faster, more predictable reviews would let California build housing and infrastructure at lower cost.
A study by Blue Sky Consulting Group, commissioned by the California Chamber of Commerce, estimates state and local governments and other public agencies would see $1.5 billion in combined savings and additional revenues.
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that state and local governments and courts would face initial costs in the high tens of millions of dollars annually, potentially more than $100 million, over the first several years, partly covered by fees.
Some costs would likely decline over time, the office said, but long-term impacts are unclear. For instance, faster building would likely lower project costs, but any harmful environmental impacts resulting from quicker reviews would cost state and local agencies more.
Carstens said the savings aren’t even guaranteed, and that the Chamber of Commerce is using the affordability debate to deregulate in favor of business.
“They say it’s about affordable housing, but that’s not anywhere visible in this measure,” Carstens said. “There’s no affordability provision or requirement for addressing the needs of people who are impoverished and underprivileged.”
If Prop. 45 passes, much would be left to the courts. The measure says it should be interpreted to give “the fullest possible weight” to approving and building essential projects. Opponents say that would tilt unclear language in favor of applicants.
Marciniak said the provision is meant for situations the authors couldn’t predict.
“There is going to be confusion, but I think importantly, a judge in California is going to look at this and understand immediately what it means,” he said.

Why are pro-housing groups split on Proposition 45?

In summary
Proposition 45 is intended to make it easier to build. But some pro-housing groups worry it will only lead to more sprawl.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
For nearly a decade, California’s Yes In My Backyard activists and other pro-development advocates have wanted to overhaul California’s signature environmental law to clear the way for more housing construction.
Now Proposition 45 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-45-environmental-review/) is on the ballot. Supporters say it would, among other things, overhaul that law, known as the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA, to clear the way for — you guessed it — more housing construction.
So why are YIMBYs divided?
Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat and one of the movement’s most stalwart champions in the Legislature, is for it. So is the bulk of the building industry (https://yesonprop45.com/our-coalition/), including many major for- and non-profit developers.
Bay Area pro-housing advocates Eastbay for Everyone (https://eastbayforeveryone.org/2026/03/05/streamlining-sprawl-is-not-pro-housing/) and the Greenbelt Alliance (https://www.greenbelt.org/blog/ceqa-baca-initiative/), two typical allies of Wicks, are emphatically against it.
In the uncommitted middle lies the lion’s share of California YIMBYism: Abundant Housing Los Angeles (https://www.abundanthousingla.org/endorsements-pac#endorsements), SPUR (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/2026-11/ca-prop-45-environmental-review-ceqa), and both California YIMBY (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-45-2026/) and YIMBY Action (https://yimbyaction.org/prop45-recap) — the movement’s two flagship advocacy organizations — have all taken neutral positions.
“It’s been a weird campaign so far,” said Ali Sapirman, advocacy manager at the Housing Action Coalition, an urban building industry group that supports the measure. “The housing community has been a little bit fractured.”
Those fissures aren’t over whether more homes should be built across California. Instead, it mostly boils down to a question of where .
“The central question here is how you feel about sprawl,” Max Dubler of California YIMBY wrote in the group’s non-endorsement statement (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-45-2026/), referring to low-density housing development at the edge of metro areas. Though some exurban growth “will necessarily be part of solving our housing shortage,” he expressed concern about making it easier to build “car-dependent sprawl housing and the freeways and water infrastructure necessary to serve that sprawl.”
To sprawl or not to sprawl
For nearly a decade, the Legislature has been on a tear (https://www.spur.org/publications/research/2026-06-30/california-housing-laws), passing “streamlining” bills aimed at speeding up the regulatory approval of new construction. Almost all of those laws have only applied to projects in places where homes and other infrastructure already exist.
Prioritizing so-called infill development helped wrangle together a coalition of developers and construction labor unions (https://calmatters.org/politics/2025/07/california-construction-unions-housing/), but also a diverse swath of Democratic-leaning advocates whose interest in seeing more apartments and condos goes beyond the cause of affordability alone. That includes climate activists who want to see less commuter car traffic; transit, bicycle and pedestrian advocates who want more riders and walkers and urbanists who want Los Angeles to more closely resemble Barcelona (https://la.streetsblog.org/2022/07/07/some-urban-observations-from-my-barcelona-vacation).
In breaking from that urban focus, Prop. 45 is driving a wedge inside that coalition.

If passed, the measure would speed up the review process required under CEQA (pronounced “see-kwah”) for all types of housing projects. That includes transit-adjacent downtown condo towers, but also freshly paved subdivisions at the metropolitan fringe.
The measure is “a doubling down on essentially 75 years of land-use patterns that we know haven’t worked,” said Jordan Grimes, legislative director with Greenbelt Alliance, which opposes the measure. “It’s a return to the sprawl era.”
Not everyone in the movement necessarily sees that as a bad thing. Among those who want California to build its way out of its current housing shortage (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/09/california-housing-shortage/), opinions differ (https://www.nytimes.com/2025/04/10/magazine/suburban-sprawl-texas.html) over whether more environmentally-friendly (https://ternercenter.berkeley.edu/research-and-policy/role-of-new-housing-in-reducing-climate-pollution/) infill development alone is up to the task.
“I’m an ‘all of the above’ person when it comes to housing,” said Wicks, explaining her support of the measure. “I think we need housing of all different types, shapes, and sizes.”
An earlier version of this rift first emerged earlier this decade when a handful of Bay Area tech investors announced plans to build a brand new city on Solano County farmland in 2023 under the banner of California Forever (https://www.nytimes.com/2023/08/25/business/land-purchases-solano-county.html). Some YIMBY commentators applauded the plan as a welcome injection of much-needed supply (https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2025-12-01/california-forever-regulatory-streamlining). Others decried it as sprawl dressed in urbanist clothing (https://sfstandard.com/2024/06/21/california-forever-east-solano-plan-yimby/).
With Prop. 45, that regional debate is now playing out at a statewide scale.
Housing front and center
Prop. 45 is about much more than housing policy (https://calmatters.org/environment/2026/10/prop-45-california-ceqa-explained/).
CEQA requires public agencies to review the possible environmental consequences of the decisions they make, including the permitting of private projects. For decades industry groups, developers and, more recently, housing supply boosters have said the law makes it too easy for project opponents to jam up worthwhile projects by repeatedly demanding additional analysis.
“The clock is endless and the number of people and entities who can challenge you are also endless,” said Linda Mandolini of Eden Housing, an affordable housing developer.
Prop. 45 would not exempt any projects from environmental review outright. But for projects deemed “essential,” it would narrow the focus of these reviews and require them to wrap up within 365 business days. Any resulting litigation would also face a shot clock; Judges would have 270 business days to resolve them. Such lawsuits would also be made harder to sustain in court. Aside from housing, essential projects include roads, hospitals, schools, clean energy projects, water and broadband infrastructure.
But housing has loomed large in the electoral debate. The Yes on 45 campaign has touted the support of affordable housing developers (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/10/02/affordable-housing-leaders-unite-behind-prop-45-to-lower-housing-costs-and-build-the-homes-californians-need/) and housing advocates (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Xg8AW0KK6tY), while pointing to housing affordability (https://www.kqed.org/news/12100915/housing-fix-or-data-center-loophole-this-ballot-measure-would-overhaul-ceqa) concerns as the initial impetus for the measure.
It’s easy to see why. Environmental challenges to often innocuous-seeming housing projects have regularly generated headlines for years, helping to cement the idea among lawmakers and many voters that CEQA is a major cause of the state’s housing woes.
Environmental justice groups and their allies have spent years fighting against that argument in the Legislature. Though Prop. 45 does not exempt “essential” projects from environmental review outright — it just shortens and hems in the process — these groups have now lined up to oppose it for much the same reason: They reject the premise that CEQA needs fixing.
But for opponents like Grimes, who supported many recent streamlining bills, the argument that the law is holding up desperately needed residential construction is a year out of date. Last year, the governor signed Assembly Bill 130 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab130), a Wicks-authored measure that exempted most infill housing (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) from the CEQA.
Since becoming law in July 2025, developers have used it to entitle 17,913 units of housing, according to the Office of Land Use and Climate Innovation, a state agency.
“When you look at what’s left to do on urban housing, there are absolutely still barriers,” said Grimes, whose organization applauded last year’s exemption (https://www.greenbelt.org/blog/ceqa-reform-ca/). “CEQA just isn’t one of them.”
The task of the No on 45 campaign, he said, is to convince enough voters that “we’ve actually solved this problem.”
Are we done here?
Many developers and affordable housing advocates, even those working in urban areas, dispute that CEQA is no longer a major obstacle.
Last year’s exemption does not exempt projects larger than 20 acres, which means supersized (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/s-f-stonestown-development-19577137.php) urban (https://nypost.com/2026/05/26/lifestyle/westminster-mall-demolished-for-bolsa-pacific-mega-complex/) redevelopment (https://www.cbsnews.com/sanfrancisco/news/development-at-cupertinos-old-vallco-shopping-mall-site-finally-moves-ahead/) projects are still subject to the old process.
Prop. 45 also applies shot clocks to other permits (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/27/what-does-baca-do-part-iv/) issued later in the development process and which regularly slow a project more than environmental review.
And while state laws like last year’s infill carveout may grant certain developers the right to ignore CEQA, there is nothing to stop a deep-pocketed opponent from suing anyway. Putting time limits on those lawsuits could be the difference between a project succeeding and being delayed to death, said Mandolini.
She points to the planned 130-unit affordable housing project that Eden Housing has been trying to and failing to build in the Bay Area suburb of Livermore since 2018 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/livermore-affordable-housing-timeline/) as an example. In 2021, a nonprofit funded by a handful of well-heeled Livermore residents sued the city, arguing that it hadn’t done enough environmental analysis on a housing development that would be built on a former grocery store parking lot behind a row of downtown restaurants. A lower court ruled that the group’s CEQA arguments were “almost utterly without merit.” An appellate court agreed. The state Supreme Court allowed that ruling to stand.
But by then two years had passed.
“Every year you lose in litigation is real money for real projects and another year that 130 families don’t get to live in that housing,” said Mandolini. “It’s a great way to kill a project.”
Even an infill project.
But among some pro-housing supporters of the proposition, the infill versus sprawl debate isn’t much of a debate at all.
“We’re not an urbanist organization,” said Mahdi Manji with the Inner City Law Center, a legal aid provider and housing advocacy group in Los Angeles’ Skid Row. The group supports Prop. 45 and doesn’t mind the concept of more housing far from the city’s core. “To the extent it results in housing that is a little more affordable in Lancaster and Palmdale, a lot of our clients live out in Lancaster and Palmdale.”

Endorsement: CEQA is a mess. Prop 45 is even messier
Proposition 45 would significantly expedite the CEQA review process for eight categories of projects and potentially make it easier to build environmentally ruinous projects.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 17, 2026
What’s the most polarizing four-letter word in California politics?
CEQA.
That wasn’t always the case. When then-Gov. Ronald Reagan signed the California Environmental Quality Act into law in 1970, the need could not have been more obvious. Californians were fed up with planners bulldozing low-income neighborhoods and communities of color for miles of polluting freeways. They were horrified by the ecological damage and habitat destruction caused by suburban sprawl. They were tired of top-down infrastructure projects that left communities feeling disempowered and voiceless.
CEQA laid out a basic protective framework: Before approving a project, government officials needed to evaluate potential negative environmental impacts and identify ways to mitigate or avoid them while providing ample opportunity for public review and input.

But it didn’t take long for the law to be easily manipulated for ends that had little or nothing to do with the environment.
NIMBYs used the process to delay new infill housing — driving up costs and reducing the likelihood projects get built. Unions leveraged CEQA to extort favorable labor terms on projects (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/california-housing-union-labor-17802611.php). Courts showed a predisposition for allowing just about anything to become grounds for a CEQA challenge — which is how we ended up with a 2022 lawsuit against a UC Berkeley housing project (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Editorial-UC-Berkeley-students-are-now-16931016.php) that effectively branded students as a form of pollution.
This editorial board has repeatedly decried CEQA abuses and has urged politicians to take decisive action (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/uc-berkeley-peoples-park-housing-ceqa-newsom-17816129.php).
In recent years, they have, to a degree.

State lawmakers passed, and Gov. Gavin Newsom signed, bills to, among other things, permit more units on many single-family-home lots (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/California-cities-rush-to-limit-new-law-16647764.php), streamline the development of dense housing near transit (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/openforum/article/sb79-now-law-fight-affordable-housing-goes-21094908.php), exempt almost all infill housing from CEQA (https://sfchronicle.com/california/article/ceqa-housing-roadblocks-newsom-20402835.php) and speed up permitting timelines for large clean-energy projects (https://modelclimatelaws.org/resources/californias-sb-205-2022/).
But it’s still far too easy to bury certain essential projects in delay, litigation and costly uncertainty.
Proposition 45 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop45-text-proposed-laws.pdf), placed on the November ballot via signatures gathered by the California Chamber of Commerce, would significantly expedite the CEQA review process for eight categories of projects (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop45-110326.pdf) its authors deem “essential”: housing, water (other than the Delta tunnel (https://www.sfchronicle.com/news/article/will-california-ever-build-the-delta-tunnel-22237021.php)), clean energy (excepting nuclear power), healthcare, public safety, wildfire mitigation, broadband internet access, education and transportation (other than high-speed rail).
How would the measure aid these kinds of projects?
First, it establishes a litany of strict deadlines — some of which are technically already in CEQA but rarely enforced. Government agencies, for example, would have 30 days to determine whether a project application is complete, 365 days to conduct an environmental review and decide whether to certify it and 90 days to decide on permits. If agencies fail to meet these deadlines, applicants could trigger a public hearing within 60 days, at which time a final decision must be made. Applicants can sue if agencies don’t follow these procedures.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 45 also significantly reduces paperwork. Government agencies could no longer repeatedly ask developers for more information to determine whether an application is complete — they would have one chance to produce an “exhaustive written corrections list.” Agencies would also be prohibited from changing the criteria or scope of their assessments mid-review. Agencies would no longer have to come up with multiple alternatives to environmentally impactful projects; instead, the applicant would propose just one alternative. The measure also restricts the public comments that can be included in the administrative record.
Finally, Prop 45 permits courts to halt only portions of a project determined to have “a specific, adverse impact upon public safety.” If courts sign off on an environmental review, no further lawsuits would be allowed. Lawsuits, including appeals, would need to be resolved within 270 days, with a possible 90-day extension.
In aggregate, these changes are far bigger in scope than any previous CEQA reform.
Some of the stipulations are eminently reasonable.
Enforcing deadlines is a no-brainer, as is eliminating excess paperwork and reducing frivolous litigation. Project applicants are not entitled to approvals, but they are entitled to decisions being made in a timely manner.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Furthermore, some of the projects Prop 45 seeks to streamline — like public transit, bike lanes and infill housing — are objectively good for the environment. They shouldn’t be subject to extreme CEQA scrutiny.
Others, however, are beyond questionable.
Prop 45 applies its streamlining process to freeway expansions and greenfield housing development in wildfire zones. And why does it specifically exempt the one transportation project that arguably needs the most help: California’s voter-approved high-speed rail, which is years behind schedule and billions over budget thanks in part to costly CEQA challenges? (https://grist.org/transportation/billions-spent-miles-to-go-the-story-of-californias-failure-to-build-high-speed-rail/)
Poll testing, said Emma Manoukian Chung, a strategist for the Yes on Prop 45 campaign. There was “voter appetite” for freeways and sprawl, but not high-speed rail.
But throwing a grab bag of poll-tested projects together and suggesting they should be evaluated on substantially similar terms is neither reasonable nor good policy.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Huge infrastructure projects — such as freeways and dams — have fundamentally different environmental impacts than infill housing. And infill housing has different environmental consequences than single-family homes in car-centric, high-wildfire-risk zones.
It makes no sense to apply the same scrutiny and deadlines to each.
It’s also unclear whether Prop 45 applies to data centers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/data-centers-artificial-intelligence-dakotas-22362642.php). Opponents insist the “broadband internet access” category leaves open the possibility, while proponents insist that it doesn’t.
Ultimately, that question will likely have to be answered through litigation — ironically, the very thing Prop 45 is trying to curb.
It’s also ironic that Prop 45, despite aiming to reduce uncertainty, actually creates much more of it.
“This is deep, deep, deep in the weeds of environmental law,” Chris Elmendorf, a UC Davis law professor and one of California’s preeminent CEQA experts, told us. “It’s a super complicated body of law that they’re trying to change, trying to make it easier to build stuff.
“Some of the changes are good and some may be bad, and who knows what kind of second-order effects they will have?”
That’s why the state Legislature is best suited to handle complicated, nuanced policy, tweaking laws as needed — unlike the all-or-nothing blunt instrument of the ballot box.
“An initiative should be considered a last resort … when the Legislature is doing nothing,” Prop 45 opponent Darrell Steinberg, a former Sacramento mayor and state Senate leader, told us. But, he said, “just the opposite” is occurring.
We agree.
Lawmakers need to craft more fundamental CEQA reforms, particularly when it comes to housing, transportation and green energy projects. Some of those solutions are contained within Prop 45.

Prop 45 is poll-tested political Swiss cheese, not a thoughtful effort to produce better outcomes. Vote no.

The California Environmental Quality Act has been used in such an abusive way for more than 50 years that then-Gov. Jerry Brown’s 2012 description of CEQA reform as “the Lord’s work” has gone from being seen as a good one-liner from an unusually witty politician to a profound observation about life in the Golden State.
There is a reason the Legislature has had to pass so many CEQA exemptions:
Many major, valuable projects would never have been built without this protection. The 1970 state law makes it too easy for third parties to block or stall proposals that they don’t like or want to be paid to support. This led directly to a 2017 analysis that documents CEQA’s central role in the state’s decades-old shortage of housing, massively driving up the cost of all types of shelter and impoverishing millions of residents.

Yes, of course, some CEQA lawsuits are defensible and necessary.
But when you see the range of organizations that have vowed support for Proposition 45 — a modest CEQA reform on the November ballot sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce — it’s eye-opening.
The California Hospital Association, the California Farm Bureau, the California Senior Alliance and more than a half-dozen clean energy groups are among a vast list of institutions seeking relief from the migraines they face because of the broadly written, vague law.
Prop. 45 would impose a 365-day limit on official environmental reviews for projects ranging from broadband construction to building roads, homes and schools to wildfire mitigation. Courts would be given a maximum of 270 days to rule on CEQA suits after they are filed.
Contrary to claims that the changes would gut “the state’s strongest-in-the-nation environmental laws,” local governments would still have considerable authority in the approval process. Activists wouldn’t be muzzled.
This is reflected in the analysis of Prop. 45 from the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.
The LAO’s biggest concern had to do with potentially substantial implementation costs for state and local governments, not weakened green regulations. And the analysis also noted the benefit to governments of new revenue from ventures no longer blocked by CEQA — and from having their own projects cost less.
Prop. 45 won’t transform the state’s regulatory maze overnight. But it would make California’s planning approval process fairer, less expensive and considerably more predictable.
Yes on 45.

Prop 45 Would Cut Roughly Three Years from the Longest Residential EIR Timelines
Estimating Prop 45’s impact on the average residential EIR entitlement timeline requires calculating the difference between (a) the status quo average entitlement duration for the EIR project sample and (b) the average period across these projects if Prop 45’s 591-day CEQA review time limit were enforced against EIR projects with review durations exceeding this maximum. Similarly, Prop 45’s impact on entitlement volatility depends on the change in the standard deviation of project entitlement periods under the 591-day limit.
Figure 7 summarizes the calculation of the change in the average entitlement duration under Prop 45. Under the status quo, the average entitlement period is an estimated 1,276 days (i.e., 1,141 days of CEQA review plus 135 days of other entitlement review). Of the 539 projects in the EIR sample, 221 had their EIRs certified in fewer than 591 days, and the average total entitlement period for this cohort (509 days) is assumed to remain the same under Prop 45. For the remaining 318 projects with CEQA reviews exceeding the Prop 45 time limit, the average status quo entitlement period is 1,809 days, of which 1,674 days is CEQA review. Prop 45’s 591-day limit would reduce the total entitlement period to 726 days, on average (as it would reduce the CEQA review phase from 1,674 days to Prop 45’s 591-day limit). As a result, Prop 45 would cut the average entitlement timeline across all residential EIR projects roughly in half, from 1,276 days to 637 days. For projects exceeding Prop 45’s time limit, the reduction would be even greater: 1,082 days, or roughly three years.

Economic and Fiscal Impacts of Increased Residential Construction
Prop 45’s Impact on Housing Affordability
By adding nearly 200,000 homes over ten years, Prop 45 would increase housing supply and put downward pressure on rents and home prices. Based on the state Department of Finance (DOF) estimates of the total statewide housing stock (https://dof.ca.gov/forecasting/demographics/estimates/e-5-population-and-housing-estimates-for-cities-counties-and-the-state-2020-2026/) (15.06 million units as of 2026) and status quo permitting rates (i.e., 108,269 units annually), the increase in residential construction under Prop 45 would increase the state’s housing stock by 1.21% after 10 years. 18 According to a recent Pew Research Center analysis, a 10% increase in a metropolitan region’s rental supply resulted in a 5.4% reduction in the region’s rents relative to nationwide rent cost trends (i.e., a “supply-price effect” of 0.54). 19 Based on this effect, Prop 45’s supply impact would reduce average rents and home prices by 0.66% (i.e., 1.21% × 0.54).
Macroeconomic Benefits of New Housing
In addition to Prop 45’s expected impact on housing costs in California, new housing also generates spillover economic and fiscal benefits that exceed the housing affordability impacts shown above. Empirical studies of supply-constrained housing markets have shown that unlocking new housing supply in high-cost regions promotes economic growth by enabling more workers to access the higher-paying jobs concentrated in these areas. 20 This expansion of the regional labor supply, in turn, attracts more firms to the area. Housing construction in high-demand regions additionally provides several quality-of-life benefits, including reduced commute times and household overcrowding. 21
Fiscal Impacts of Increased Residential Development
Increases in residential development generate additional tax revenues for state and local governments on a one-time basis during the construction period and on an ongoing annual basis once the new units are complete. Construction period tax revenues include personal income taxes (PIT) generated by income earned by construction workers and firm owners, corporation taxes generated by the corporate profits from this activity, and sales taxes on construction materials and equipment. Ongoing property tax revenues are generated annually once a new unit is added to the local property tax roll.

IV. Non-Residential Impacts
By shortening non-residential project review timelines, Prop 45 would lower costs incurred by public agencies and California utility ratepayers or consumers. Longer project review periods increase total project costs through two primary channels. First, because the costs of pre-development activities, including planning, engineering, design, and environmental review, are incurred before construction begins, longer review periods impose higher carrying costs on sponsors (i.e., the “pre-development cost of capital”). Second, because construction costs have historically outpaced general inflation in California, delaying the start of construction imposes higher real construction costs on project developers (i.e., “construction cost inflation”).
Pre-Development Cost Impact
Project sponsors require a minimum annual rate of return on pre-development capital investments. The impact of these capital costs on total project budgets depends on the project sponsor type as well as the share of project expenses incurred during the pre-development period.
Public Agency and Private Sector Pre-Development Costs of Capital
For private sponsors, the cost of capital reflects the annual internal rate of return (IRR) required by a project’s investors or lenders. Because of the high risk of project failure during the planning and approval process, 27 higher rates of return are demanded on pre-development stage capital than capital invested in shovel-ready projects. Because clean energy projects account for roughly 63% of total IOU and private sector essential project expenditures, and 100% of the annual essential construction spending incurred by California’s ratepayers, this report relies on market study estimates of the IRR typically earned on pre-development utility-scale solar project investments. 28 Based on this research, the real private sponsor cost of capital is an estimated 16%. 29
Though public agencies may not require or earn investment returns on their infrastructure spending, these entities may incur financing costs to the extent bonds are issued to fund these initial capital investments. In either case, given the time value of money, governments discount projects’ future benefits or costs when conducting benefit-cost analyses (i.e., for every year that a project or program’s benefits are delayed, their expected values are reduced by the chosen discount rate). 30 Given the large share of public spending on transportation projects, this report adopts a discount rate of 4% as the effective public agency cost of capital. 31
Impact of Pre-Development Capital Costs Across Essential Project Categories
The per-year pre-development cost for each essential project category and project sponsor type is calculated by applying the discount rate or IRR (an annual percentage) to the percentage share of project expenses committed during pre-development (i.e., the pre-development cost share).
As shown in Figure 17, based on federal survey data and research materials, this cost share is estimated to range from 3% (for clean energy projects) to 25% (for broadband). 32 As a result, a one-year reduction in the average transportation project review period, for example, is estimated to reduce total project costs by 0.6% if the sponsor is a public agency (i.e., 15% × 4%) and by 2.4% if the sponsor is a private firm (i.e., 15% × 16%).

**Considering user preferences in policy choices**

I want to ensure the user requests a choice rather than a preference, focusing on generally accepted reforms. However, this suggestion risks going too far. While there are potential regulatory advantages to not requiring "affordable housing," we shouldn't overlook the importance of demand statutes in reducing bills. I need to understand the standards that prevent shifting goals, as a review in 18 months may require updated scientific hazard information. Also, the sweeping exclusion regarding indigenous harm feels unjust, and proposed changes could conflict with clean energy goals.

Prop
45
CA
Prop
45
|
Statute
Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects
Changes the California Environmental Quality Act to streamline the environmental review of eight categories of housing and certain transportation, energy, health, public safety, education, and water projects designated as essential.
SPUR's Recommendation
The SPUR Board of Directors could not reach a supermajority consensus position on this measure. SPUR agrees that CEQA creates excessive risk, cost, uncertainty, and delay and has consistently supported targeted reforms for infill housing, clean energy, and climate resilience. However, Prop. 45 would make broader changes that conflict with SPUR’s vision for urban growth. The measure could accelerate desirable projects, such as infill housing near transit and zero-emission energy infrastructure, but it could also streamline development that contributes to sprawl or environmental harm, including subdivisions on the urban edge and polluting energy facilities. Given weak growth controls and lower land costs at the urban edge, Prop. 45's provisions could encourage development patterns that undermine the measure’s benefits and SPUR’s mission. Prop. 45 could reduce frivolous litigation and delays by strengthening evidentiary standards and establishing deadlines. However, its timelines could strain local governments, and potential lawsuits could discourage legitimate planning decisions. Finally, the law would be difficult to modify, requiring voter approval or a two-thirds legislative majority.
The SPUR Board of Directors supports removing excessive risk, uncertainty, and delay from building infill housing, public transit, drinking water, hospitals, schools, and truly zero-emission infrastructure in the right places, but it remains deeply concerned about this measure’s potential negative impacts.
No Recommendation
What Prop. 45 Would Do
Proposition 45 would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to streamline environmental review for eight categories of projects it deems “essential,” regardless of location or scale, as well as any related public, private, or utility infrastructure. It would limit the scope of environmental analysis, create shorter, enforceable timelines, narrow court discretion, and provide project applicants with new enforcement remedies.
“Essential” projects are described as:
Housing projects , defined as residential units, emergency shelters, transitional housing, supportive housing, farmworker housing, mixed-use developments, student housing, group living accommodations, and senior housing
Clean energy projects that produce, generate, or store electricity derived from renewable or sustainable resources, including but not limited to solar, wind, geothermal, fuel cells, small hydroelectric generation, digester gas, biomass, landfill gas, ocean wave, ocean thermal, or tidal current, and associated transmission lines
Water projects, including those that directly or indirectly provide water to a public water system
Public health projects , defined as medical treatment facilities
Public safety projects, defined as first-responder facilities or wildfire reduction projects undertaken by a public agency, including home hardening and vegetation management and electric utility line replacement, hardening, or undergrounding
Broadband Internet access projects, defined as projects to provide mass market retail Internet service to customers, such as data centers
Transportation projects, including public streets, highways, bridges, transit projects, and electric vehicle charging and refueling infrastructure
Education facilities, including their acquisition and expansion
Projects eligible for streamlining would include new construction, improvements, maintenance, repair, or replacement projects. Projects not eligible for streamlining under this measure include jail or detention facilities, new oil or natural gas production facilities, the California high-speed rail system, and the Delta conveyance project.
Prop 45 would make the following key changes to CEQA environmental review:
Enforceable timelines for environmental review: Currently, the timeline for certifying an environmental review depends on the project’s complexity and the staff workload at the responsible public agency (the “lead agency”). Prop. 45 would establish the following enforceable timelines for the certification of an environmental review:
30 days to determine whether an application is complete
180 days to approve a negative declaration (when a project has no environmental impacts) or mitigated negative declaration (when a project’s environmental impacts can be mitigated)
365 days to certify an environmental impact report
If a lead public agency misses these deadlines or imposes unlawful conditions on the project, applicants may file a legal complaint within 90 days to compel a decision and may require the lead agency to convene its highest-ranking governing body to vote on the project application.
Public comment: Prop. 45 would cap public comment periods for essential projects at 45 days for draft environmental impact reports and 20 days for negative or mitigated negative declarations.
Scope of environmental review: The measure would narrow the scope of the environmental impact report for essential projects and give project applicants greater discretion. Key changes include:
Optional scoping: Makes the scoping phase of environmental impact reports optional. If the project applicant pursues scoping, the lead agency must complete it within 60 days, including the mandatory 30-day public comment period.
Limited alternatives: Restricts the review to a single project alternative selected by the applicant, shifting planning responsibility from the lead agency to the developer.
Legal challenges: Makes several changes to reduce frivolous legal challenges and risk of delays.
Filing limitations: Requires lawsuits to be filed within 30 days of project approval.
Substantial evidence: Increases the standard of review from “fair argument” to “substantial evidence,” creating a higher standard for challenging the lead agency’s decision and reducing frivolous lawsuits.
Judicial “shot clock” : Requires courts to resolve lawsuits within 270 days.
Judicial discretion: Directs courts to require applicants to correct rejected portions of an environmental impact report but not to redo the entire report.
The Backstory
The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), enacted in 1970, requires state and local public agencies to evaluate, disclose, and mitigate the potential environmental impacts of public and private projects that require government approval, use public funds, and could physically change the environment. CEQA currently applies to most projects, except some types of infill housing and transportation projects within existing cities and within walking distance to transit.
CEQA is a foundation of California environmental protection, helping preserve natural resources and prevent harmful projects in disadvantaged communities. However, its review and litigation processes can also add significant time and cost to housing and infrastructure projects and have been used to block infill housing, transit, and other projects.
In recent years, California has sought to preserve CEQA’s protections while addressing the state’s significant need for affordable housing and climate-friendly transportation options by streamlining or exempting certain infill housing, affordable housing, and sustainable transportation projects through legislative action. Despite these reforms, the housing affordability crisis has worsened. Prop. 45 would pursue broader CEQA reforms directly through the ballot.
The California Chamber of Commerce placed the measure on the ballot through a voter signature initiative. It requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass and would take effect immediately. If enacted, amendments would require a two-thirds vote of the state legislature.
Equity Impacts
Prop. 45 would pose three main negative equity impacts. First, it could streamline projects that increase pollution and toxic exposures in environmental justice communities — those with an unfair share of pollution, health risks, and climate hazards — including certain renewable energy facilities and ancillary infrastructure such as highway expansions.
Second, it would limit required consultation with federally recognized tribes, excluding more than 50 state-recognized tribes and disempowering many tribes that lack sufficient documentation to become federally recognized.
Third, it would cap public comment periods (45 days for full environmental impact reports), which may be insufficient for large or complex projects. A short comment period tends to favor those commenters who are well-organized and well-resourced.
Pros
Prop. 45 could reduce project delays and costs by addressing routine administrative burdens, resolving legal ambiguity, providing greater certainty, and potentially speeding housing approvals and construction.
Expedited review could accelerate safety projects such as undergrounding power lines, helping prevent loss of life and property damage while controlling ratepayer costs.
Requiring substantial evidence of harm could raise the legal standard and make frivolous lawsuits easier to dismiss, potentially speeding up approval and construction.
Cons
The measure’s broad scope could streamline environmentally harmful projects or worsen conditions in environmental justice communities, regardless of location or scale.
Streamlining low-density, greenfield, hazard-prone, and auto-oriented development could encourage sprawl, including through highway expansions, gas pipelines, and fueling stations.
Allowing lawsuits over project denials and conditions could undermine local planning powers, increase litigation risk, and discourage agencies from regulating projects with significant impacts.
Strict review timelines could burden resource-constrained agencies, particularly smaller cities, and increase litigation risk. Strict public comment timelines may make it harder for people with fewer resources to participate.
Allowing environmental reviews to analyze only one applicant-selected alternative could limit consideration of better options.
Requiring a two-thirds legislative vote for amendments could make the law difficult to adapt or improve.
No Recommendation

Proposition 45: No Recommendation
September 23, 2026
Share
Share this page on Twitter (https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcayimby.org%2Fblog%2Fproposition-45-2026%2F&text=Proposition+45%3A+%3Cspan+class%3D%22dewidow%22%3ENo+Recommendation%3C%2Fspan%3E)
Share this page on Facebook (https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fcayimby.org%2Fblog%2Fproposition-45-2026%2F&t=Proposition%2045:%20No%20Recommendation)
Share this page via Email (mailto:?subject=Proposition+45%3A+%3Cspan+class%3D%22dewidow%22%3ENo+Recommendation%3C%2Fspan%3E+-+California+YIMBY&body=https%3A%2F%2Fcayimby.org%2Fblog%2Fproposition-45-2026%2F)
by Max Dubler
Introduction
While Proposition 45 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/index.htm) meaningfully touches on housing, it will have a much more significant impact on non-housing projects. Pro-housing voters should consider the arguments for and against the measure and make their own decision based on their values.
Analysis
Background: The California Environmental Quality Act
Passed in 1970 and signed into law by then-Governor Reagan, the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA, say “SEE-kwah”) required government agencies to study and publicize the potential environmental impacts of public projects like dams, highways, and power plants, and gave the public the right to sue if they do not believe the impact analysis is sufficient. The scope of the law was massively expanded when the courts ruled that any project that requires public approval is a “public project.” This empowered a wide variety of interests to use the CEQA process to delay or block projects they don’t like.
Last year, the state legislature passed AB 130 (https://cayimby.org/legislation/ab-609/), which exempted (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) “infill” housing, broadly defined [1] as homes in existing developed areas, from environmental review under CEQA. This was a major victory for California YIMBY, which has long sought this exemption and sponsored AB 609, which was incorporated into AB 130.
What does Prop 45 do?
Creates an alternative, opt-in process with strict “shot clocks” for environmental review (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-local-timelines) for “essential” housing, water, transportation ( excluding high speed rail), clean energy, transmission, broadband, and healthcare infrastructure. Environmental review for these projects must be completed within 365 business days, or about a year and a half. There are shorter timelines for determining application completeness (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-completeness) (30 days) and lesser levels of environmental review (180 days for a negative declaration or a mitigated negative declaration).
Creates a 90-day shot clock for “any and all” public agency approvals required for essential projects besides CEQA, including building permits, Coastal Development Permits, and utility approvals.
Requires tribal consultation for all projects, AB 130 labor standards for housing projects (except 100% affordable projects under 85’), and Section 21183.5 labor standards (https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-prc/division-13/chapter-6-5/section-21183-5/) for other projects that use this environmental review pathway.
Limits public comment on environmental reviews to 45 days (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-public-comment).
Limits the scope of “alternative projects” that must be analyzed (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-alternatives) in the environmental review process to one alternative proposed by the applicant and a “no project” alternative.
Creates a new evidentiary standard for environmental impacts (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-impacts) requiring that they only be found significant if they violate objective, quantifiable standards already in existing law (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-judicial-scope) when a project is proposed, and freezes those standards on the date a project application is filed (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-impacts). This would eliminate public agencies’ broad discretion to explore project alternatives and negotiate environmental mitigations.
Curtails (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-remedies) courts’ ability to block projects in their entirety. If a legal challenge to a project’s environmental review is successful, the remedy is limited to the specific issue identified in the lawsuit. The courts can’t order an agency to rescind its approval of the broader project.
Broadly, Prop 45 tightens up the environmental review process. It will make it easier to build infrastructure and other large scale projects by curtailing potential litigants’ ability to slow down and block construction by filing lawsuits challenging projects’ environmental impact analyses.
How does this affect housing?
Prop 45 would affect housing in two major ways: first, it would make it easier to build housing projects [2], mostly new subdivisions, that do not qualify for the AB 130 infill exemption, as well as the infrastructure necessary to service those housing projects. Second, it would significantly speed public agency approvals for housing projects that use this environmental review process.
The labor provisions in AB 130, the existing CEQA infill exemption, would apply (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-housing-labor) to projects that use the Prop 45 environmental review process unless (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-mandatory-parts) they are also using a different streamlining law that mandates prevailing wages or a project labor requirement, in which case they would have to abide by those requirements.
While Prop 45 will speed public agency approvals for all housing, it will also make it easier to build car-dependent sprawl housing and the freeways and water infrastructure necessary to serve that sprawl.
What does California YIMBY think of this?
While this measure does affect housing, it’s not primarily about housing. Rather, it’s about reining in an out of control CEQA process (https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/archive/2021/03/signature-environmental-law-hurts-housing/618264/) that has ballooned far beyond what the legislature intended in 1970 and made building large projects slow and expensive (https://www.mercurynews.com/2025/04/20/ceqa-california-high-speed-rail/?share=aft0p2r22rr2itegarfi).
Prop 45 would reform CEQA by bringing policy ideas that have worked to streamline housing permitting—shot clocks, objective standards that vest at the time of an application, limited agency discretion to expand the scope of review, narrow remedies, etc—to the environmental review process.
Whether this is a good idea depends on how you weigh the tradeoffs: is permitting new wind and solar energy infrastructure faster worth making it easier to build freeways? Should we make it easier to build transmission lines to carry that clean energy to consumers, even if it means potentially impacting wildlife habitat? Zooming out, is litigation about the public disclosure of environmental impacts (https://history.yale.edu/publications/public-citizens-attack-big-government-and-remaking-american-liberalism) really the best way to weigh the environmental costs of large projects against their potential public benefits and ensure that communities have a voice in what’s built near them?
These are big fundamental questions about growth, sustainability, and the proper structure of democratic decision-making.
Narrowing the focus to housing, the central question here is how you feel about sprawl. California YIMBY works to make it easier to build new homes in our existing cities and towns, where we already have infrastructure to serve them. As we have said before (https://cayimby.org/news-events/statement-in-support-of-the-east-solano-plan/):
“When it comes to solving our housing crisis, our focus remains on making it easier to build housing in existing cities—near quality jobs and public services. Toward this end, we have worked to liberalize (https://cayimby.org/reports/california-adu-reform-a-retrospective/) zoning, streamline (https://cayimby.org/legislation/sb-330/) permitting, and reduce (https://cayimby.org/legislation/ab-2097/) costs. We believe we can (and must) solve the housing and climate crises simultaneously. That means building communities with denser housing and alternatives to automobile dependence.”
That said, we support building well-designed new cities (https://cayimby.org/news-events/statement-in-support-of-the-east-solano-plan/) and we realize that some greenfield development will necessarily be part of solving our housing shortage. Given the scale of the housing crisis, we need all the new housing we can get. Further, lots of people want single family homes on larger lots; and they should be able to have them, to the extent that is sustainable and feasible.
Still, our friends in the environmental movement have raised significant substantive concerns (https://www.greenbelt.org/blog/ceqa-baca-initiative/) about this measure. Most relevant to housing voters: we should not be building new homes in the fire-prone wildland urban interface (https://cayimby.org/blog/the-impact-of-land-use-planning-on-wildfire-risk-a-study-in-southern-california/) because doing so puts people in harm’s way (https://cayimby.org/blog/how-the-northwests-wildfire-crisis-is-a-sprawl-crisis/) and exacerbates our insurance crisis (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-07-22/californians-are-subsidizing-mansion-wildfire-insurance-as-fair-risk-explodes). The fact that Prop 45 makes it easier to build freeways but not high speed rail also gives us pause.
The bottom line: there are good reasons to support this measure and good reasons to oppose it. Housing voters should consider it in light of broader concerns about climate and sustainability.
Recommendation: Neutral
Further Reading
Ballotpedia analysis (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_45,_Changes_to_Environmental_Review_Process_for_Certain_Projects_Initiative_(2026)), “yes” endorsement from Circulate Planning and Policy (https://www.circulatesd.org/why_circulate_supports_prop_45), “no” endorsement from Greenbelt Alliance (https://www.greenbelt.org/blog/ceqa-baca-initiative/), annotated measure text from GrowSF (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/), Legislative Analyst’s Office analysis (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026), Public Citizens: The Attack on Big Government and the Remaking of American Liberalism (https://history.yale.edu/publications/public-citizens-attack-big-government-and-remaking-american-liberalism) (book)
Notes
[1] AB 130 defines an “infill” project as one where the project site meets any of the following criteria:
(A) Has been previously developed with an urban use.
(B) At least 75 percent of the perimeter of the site adjoins parcels that are developed with urban uses.
(C) At least 75 percent of the area within a one-quarter mile radius of the site is developed with urban uses.
(D) For sites with four sides, at least three out of four sides are developed with urban uses and at least two-thirds of the perimeter of the site adjoins parcels that are developed with urban uses.
”Urban use” means any current or previous residential or commercial development, public institution, or public park that is surrounded by other urban uses, parking lot or structure, transit or transportation passenger facility, or retail use, or any combination of those uses.
[2] The measure’s definition of “essential housing projects” is extremely broad, encompassing residential projects; mixed-use projects; transitional housing, emergency shelters, and supportive housing; farmworker housing; group living accommodations like monasteries; student housing of all types; senior housing; new subdivisions; and adaptive reuse of commercial buildings.

What does BACA do? Part IV
Proposed CEQA ballot initiative changes permit approval procedures for all California laws, not just CEQA.
This is the fourth in a series of blog posts on the California Chamber of Commerce’s proposed ballot initiative (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf) amending the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). The first blog post is here (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/25/what-does-the-building-an-affordable-california-act-do/). The second blog post is here (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/26/what-does-baca-do-part-ii/). The third blog post is here (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/26/what-does-baca-do-part-iii/).
The initiative also changes all permitting procedures for any state agency and any state law for any covered “essential” project. As a result, all agencies reviewing any permit applications for covered projects will have to comply with the new procedures outlined in the initiative, even if there is no connection at all with CEQA for the project.
Again, the scope of the initiative makes clear it is not limited to CEQA: Proposed new Section 21013 states that it applies to covered “essential” projects, but with no limitation with respect to CEQA. And proposed new Section 21014(c) states that the requirements of the initiative “shall apply to review and processing of any and every application or approval for an essential project and its accompanying land use entitlements , including without limitation, discretionary adjudicative and legislative land use entitlements triggering programmatic, plan-level, or project-level environmental review under this division.” (emphasis added). Thus, while the last clause is limited to CEQA (“this division”), the first clause is most definitely not. And as I’ve pointed out earlier, the initiative calls for it to be broadly interpreted to advance approval of projects, and to override any conflicts of any other laws.
Thus, all the new procedures laid out in the initiative are not limited simply to CEQA review, but also to every other regulatory component that might apply to a covered project, even if that covered project has no CEQA component. (The applicant can opt out of the new procedures if they wish. The main reasons they might do so are because covered projects must do a tribal consultation process, and must meet minimum wage requirements or union-employment requirements for construction.)
Those new procedures include: a 90 day timeframe for reviewing applications for completeness, with a deemed approved requirement if that timeframe is not met by the agency (proposed new Section 21017); a 90 day timeframe for most project approvals that do not trigger CEQA (this timeframe results from the interaction of proposed new Section 21019(d), which requires determination of whether a project is exempt within 90 days of a project application has been deemed complete, and proposed new Section 21023(a)(1) which requires final agency decisions to be concurrent with the determination of exemption under CEQA – there are some exemptions that add up to 90 more days to this timeframe). I am … skeptical that a 90 to 180 day timeframe for all agency project reviews that do not involve CEQA is going to be workable.
But again, these fundamentally change the processes that all agencies manage approvals for all state laws – despite the initiative’s claim that it does not change other state laws.

## Proposed CEQA ballot initiative would prevent changing environmental standards very early in the development process.
This is the third in a series of blog posts on the California Chamber of Commerce’s proposed ballot initiative amending the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA).
...
The most sweeping change in the initiative is buried in the lead-in to an innocuously titled section, proposed new Section 21023 “Other Public Agency Actions for Essential Projects.”
Here is the key text, in the beginning of 21023(a)
> “If an essential project requires any other public agency action that is not expressly addressed by other provisions of this chapter, the public agency shall make a final written decision thereon based on compliance with existing laws.”
What this means is that any approval – *even if it has nothing to do with CEQA *– must be made pursuant to “compliance with existing laws.”
What does “existing laws” mean?
That term is defined in proposed new Section 21028(r)(1):
> “Formally adopted legal requirements contained in statutes, regulations, rules, standards, or ordinances that existed and were in effect on the date an application for an essential project was submitted to a public agency.”
Thus, only the law in place at the time an application is submitted to an agency can be applied to review of a project.

## An overview of my analyses of Proposition 45
I’ve written a lot on the Cal Chamber sponsored initiative to dramatically change CEQA, BACA, which is Proposition 45 on this year’s ballot.
Here are some key takeaways from what I’ve written, as well as links to the relevant blog posts.
First, BACA will not just apply to CEQA.
It broadly expands vested rights and imposes strict time limits for all permitting in the state for covered projects.
It’s possible that it prevents ever increasing or changing regulatory standards for a covered project, even after it is constructed and is in operation.
And it will significantly weaken a range of substantive environmental protections in California, such as for endangered species habitat and cumulative air pollution.
